noticias.titulo: US too focused on Middle East and not pushing Russia hard enough, Zelensky tells BBC
noticias.resumen: Ukraine's president voices frustration with US and says it is "strange" Trump has described Vladimir Putin as a friend.
noticias.texto:
US too focused on Middle East and not pushing Russia hard enough, Zelensky tells BBC
- Published
Volodymyr Zelensky has voiced deep frustration with the US, saying that delays in delivering vital anti-ballistic missiles are costing Ukrainian lives and complaining that the US is not pushing Russia hard enough during peace talks.
In an interview with the BBC at his central Kyiv office, Ukraine's president also said it was "strange" that Donald Trump had posted a picture of himself embracing Vladimir Putin as "my friend".
"Of course it's up to the President of the United States, but... it's strange," Zelensky said, speaking in English.
"He's an aggressor, and a killerâ¦He can't be a friend. Just cannot be," he said, suggesting it was like saying you were friends with Adolf Hitler during WWII.
Since a bruising encounter with Trump in the Oval Office in 2025, Zelensky has been careful how he handles relations with the United States.
Trump's two envoys have been trying to negotiate a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine - to end the huge loss of life. But they often seem more in tune with Moscow's position, than that of Kyiv.
The latest round of peace talks, mediated in Abu Dhabi earlier this month, made no obvious progress: "The more we know, the more problems", is how Zelensky described it.
He said talks were expected to resume in December.
On Thursday, Donald Trump posted on his Truth Social platform that at his own summit with Putin in China last week he had urged Russia to "pull back all military aggression against territories throughout Europe" and said he believed a peace deal with Ukraine was "a strong possibility".
But from its public statements, Russia appears to have regressed to its initial, hardline negotiating positions â on everything.
And Zelensky revealed that it was not clear whether European negotiators would be at the table, as the US envoys had announced.
The Kremlin appears to be resisting.
- Europe ready for talks with Russia on ending war in Ukraine, leaders say 
  - Published7 days ago
- Zelensky says Putin is a 'killer' after Trump calls Russian leader a friend 
  - Published5 days ago
Ukraine urgently needs the talks to move forward and bring five exhausting years of Russia's full-scale invasion to an end.
Russian strikes across the country have been growing more frequent and more deadly: the number of civilians being killed is at an all-time high.
So Zelensky called for "real helpful allies, who can push Russia" to achieve results and urged the US to live up to its reputation as a strong country with "power and respect".
"When you try to be very neutral with the aggressor... it means you support victims and you support also aggressor. It's not right," he said.
The US argues that it is neutral: in the complex search for a peace deal between the two sides that can hold.
In the meantime, Kyiv is struggling to defend its skies.
The air alerts, day and night, are now a draining feature of everyday life. As Russian ballistic missiles target power stations and bridges, jet-powered drones are launched daily at central Kyiv and other big cities.
Ukraine launches hundreds of drones at targets in Russia in response.
Zelensky said the military here are now able to destroy about 70% of Russia's fastest drones, a statistic he said was improving.
But there is a "very, very big" deficit of interceptors to stop ballistic missiles and he said the Amercians were delaying deliveries of its Patriot systems.
"It's a pity they made a focus on Middle East and they help them moreâ¦ It's a pity. We have huge questions with this," Zelensky said.
"The deficit of these missiles - that is people's lives."
He also confirmed that the US satellite communications system, Starlink â and its military version, Starshield â were still being restricted in occupied areas of Ukraine.
Ukrainian drone units have described their problems to the BBC, as their interceptor drones can no longer catch up with Russian Shaheds. It means those weapons then fly deeper into Ukraine, unhindered.
So whose decision was that?
"Technically SpaceX, politically - I don't know, I really don't know," Zelensky replied. "It's like... ping pong. We are asking one side, they say it's the other."
Tough winter
Ukraine's own long-range strikes against Russian targets have increased in recent weeks, including oil refineries and ships carrying weapons or fuel.
On Thursday, Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said an attack that sank a Russian warship docked in eastern Libya this week risked spreading war to the Mediterranean, which was unacceptable.
Zelensky defended the move, calling the warship Merkury an "absolutely fair goal".
He accepted that such strikes were "very dangerous" but said Ukraine's forces "never attack" without co-ordinating with its partners.
He declined to be more specific.
But he acknowledged that Ukraine was bracing for a difficult and dangerous winter.
Recent attacks on Kyiv have targeted bridges over the vast river Dnipro, apparently trying to cut the city in two.
Some residents have already left town for the winter and businesses closed, as power cuts and strikes on logistics networks have pushed operating costs unmanageably high.
They have also plunged much of the city into darkness.
"[Russia] wants us to run away, of course," Zelensky said.
"People can go, but we will try to defend our capital in any way. We need our capital. Without a capital, you don't have a country."

noticias.titulo: Watch: Roofs torn off and streets under water as severe weather hits US
noticias.resumen: Hundreds of thousands have been affected by storms in the country as the Thanksgiving holiday weekend begins.
noticias.texto:
Watch: Roofs torn off and streets under water as severe weather hits US
Powerful storms are battering both US coasts as the Thanksgiving holiday weekend gets under way.
Hundreds of flights have been cancelled and hundreds of thousands are without power, in states including Virginia, North Carolina and New Jersey.
Strong winds have blown roofs off houses and floodwater has submerged streets.

noticias.titulo: New Zealand's ruling coalition falls short of parliamentary majority by one seat
noticias.resumen: The right-leaning ruling bloc led by the National Party has fallen short of the majority needed to govern.
noticias.texto:
New Zealand's ruling coalition falls short of parliamentary majority by one seat
- Published
New Zealand's ruling coalition has fallen short of a parliamentary majority by one seat, following a campaign shaped by a sluggish economy and disillusioned voters.
It now needs the support of the centrist Opportunity Party to remain in power. If they cannot reach a deal, the country may have to go back to the polls.
The incumbent National Party led by Prime Minister Christopher Luxon secured 40 out of 130 seats, while its coalition partners ACT and New Zealand First took 13 and 12 respectively.
A government led by the centre-left Labour Party is not possible, official results on Friday show, as the bloc would not have enough seats even if Opportunity threw its weight behind it.
Labour secured 36 seats, The Greens took 17, while Te PÄti MÄori, which represents MÄori interests, picked up five.
Opportunity, which has been described as this election's kingmaker, secured seven seats. Opportunity's leader Qiulae Wong told reporters her party will negotiate with National, but that all options remain on the table.
"There are seven parties in parliment and everyone is responsible for making sure we do everything we can to deliver a stable government for New Zealand. It's not just up to us," she said on Friday.
Preliminary results on 7 November, election day, had projected that National combined with its coalition partners would have a slim lead over the left-leaning bloc.
But today's official tally shows it had lost two seats on special votes - cast by citizens who were overseas or outside of their registered electorate on election day - which typically skew left.
Some of National's key election pledges include lower taxes, cheaper energy, more renewable generation, and a greater focus on defence.
Labour, meanwhile, had campaigned to cut healthcare, public transport and fuel costs, more government support for social housing, among other things.
New Zealand's mixed-member proportional voting system means most governments are coalitions. Each voter makes two choices â for the representative of their constituency in parliament and a political party.
In earlier interviews with the BBC, many voters had expressed frustration over spiralling costs of living and high unemployment across the country, with declining faith in their political leadership.
"There's this kind of apathy and a bit of dread," said 21-year-old Imogen Vlutger.
A 40-year-old man said he didn't vote as he could not bring himself to tick any of the boxes on the ballot paper.
More than half of the country no longer see New Zealand as a land of opportunity, according to a survey by the Helen Clark Foundation, a public policy think tank.
Kiwis have been leaving the country in record numbers, with many of them, including former prime minister Jacinda Arden, moving to Australia.

noticias.titulo: Zelensky questions 'strange' Trump-Putin friendship in BBC interview
noticias.resumen: The Ukrainian president tells the BBC that Russia's Vladimir Putin should not be treated as a friend.
noticias.texto:
Zelensky questions 'strange' Trump-Putin friendship in BBC interview
Volodymyr Zelensky has voiced his frustration with the United States and questioned Donald Trump's relationship with Vladimir Putin in an interview with the BBC.
In a picture posted to Truth Social on Saturday, where Trump and Putin embrace, the US president described his Russian counterpart as "my friend".
"Of course it's up to the President of the United States, but... it's strange," Zelensky told the BBC's Sarah Rainsford at his office in central Kyiv.
"He [Putin] is an aggressor, and a killerâ¦He can't be a friend. Just cannot be."

noticias.titulo: My dad's watch stopped the moment he died - I found it in the ashes of Hong Kong tower fire
noticias.resumen: The city marks a year since a huge blaze tore through seven apartment blocks, killing 168 people.
noticias.texto:
My dad's watch stopped the moment he died - I found it in the ashes of Hong Kong tower fire
Mr So's parents, both in their 80s, were among the 168 people killed in last year's Hong Kong tower-block blaze - the deadliest the city had seen in decades.
Their building was the first of the Wang Fuk Court complex to catch fire, and their bodies were burned beyond recognition.
In this video Mr So, who is only using his surname, visits his parents' grave and shows what is left of his parents' possessions.
Video by Phoebe Kong and Yik Lam, BBC Chinese
Editor: Brigitte Pu

noticias.titulo: Death-sentenced Sheikh Hasina's planned return puts Bangladesh on edge - and India in a bind
noticias.resumen: The ousted prime minister's December homecoming plan deepens Dhaka-Delhi tensions and risks fresh unrest.
noticias.texto:
Death-sentenced Sheikh Hasina's planned return puts Bangladesh on edge - and India in a bind
- Published
Sheikh Hasina has repeatedly vowed to return to Bangladesh.
Now the ousted prime minister has put a date on her homecoming - 16 December - and even outlined how she intends to make the journey.
The government in Dhaka, which had previously dismissed the prospect, is taking her latest declaration more seriously.
Hasina, 79, who fled to Delhi in August 2024 after a student-led uprising ended her 15-year rule, plans to go back on Victory Day, the anniversary of Bangladesh's triumph over Pakistan in the 1971 liberation war, her spokesperson said.
She was sentenced to death after being convicted of crimes against humanity for her role in the crackdown, in a trial held in her absence that raised questions about due process. Her Awami League party is banned in Bangladesh. The UN says as many as 1,400 people were killed by security forces during the uprising.
The government says she would be arrested immediately if she returned and has promised to carry out the death sentence.
Hasina now wants the Bangladesh government to arrange a flight from Delhi. If that fails, she could travel commercially or cross the land border.
"She is even prepared to walk into Bangladesh," Abu Obaidha Arin, a key aide to Hasina, told the BBC.
India and Bangladesh share a 4,096km (2,545 mile) border across five Indian states - West Bengal, Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram. Her supporters, Arin said, had identified nine possible crossing points. "This is a carefully thought-out, precise plan. This is serious."
Dhaka has responded with defiance, insisting Hasina must be extradited.
"Reality and desire are different things," Humaiun Kobir, Bangladesh's state minister for foreign affairs, told reporters in Dhaka. "[The reality is] she's not a regular commercial passenger. She can only be brought back in handcuffs."
India's foreign ministry said on Wednesday that Hasina's extradition request was being examined through the "established process", adding that a voluntary return would be a separate matter.
Many in Dhaka believe Hasina's declaration is more than a promise of homecoming.
They believe it is an attempt to test the government's authority, force her way back into the political conversation and exploit divisions among the parties that united to oust her. It also threatens to turn India's unresolved problem of sheltering a former ally into a more immediate diplomatic crisis.
The date is significant. Hasina is invoking Victory Day to reclaim her place in Bangladesh's founding narrative. Aides say she has spent months trying to keep her party alive in exile.
Arin says Hasina has been in regular contact with party leaders and workers through interactive audio conversations on Telegram, keeping alive a network that might otherwise have been difficult to sustain from exile.
Over the past 18 months, he says, she has held more than 300 such meetings, reaching supporters across all 64 districts and the country's 300 constituencies. They are organised through the Awami League's 78 units and "can last four or five hours".
The meetings allow Hasina to listen directly to party workers, hear their grievances and understand what is happening on the ground, Arin says. He insists the response has been substantial and claims the party "could mobilise five million people to welcome her along the route from the border to Dhaka, forming a human chain".
"We have the organisational capacity to make that happen," he says.
That may be an ambitious claim. The Awami League remains a mass party with millions of supporters, but it is banned and largely shut out of mainstream politics. Much of its leadership is abroad, in jail or underground. Police have arrested supporters and filed thousands of cases against party workers.
Yet its supporters have continued to take to the streets, staging flash protests that have grown more frequent and confrontational in recent months.
Several districts have reported bomb attacks, arson and vandalism, though responsibility for some incidents remains disputed.
Gopalganj, Hasina's ancestral district, has proved particularly difficult for the authorities to control.
Awami League supporters have attacked police stations, external, torched vehicles and targeted homes and offices belonging to ruling Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) leaders, reports say. Highways have been blocked, external with felled trees and burning tyres, bringing traffic to a standstill. In some areas, police have withdrawn, external amid fears of further attacks.
Supporters have staged 40 demonstrations and more than 140 riots up to 23 November, according to data from conflict monitoring group Acled (Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project). At least 11 people, including two civilians, have been killed in political violence this month, six directly linked to the unrest, the group says.
The party's ability to cause disruption, however, is not necessarily evidence of a broad resurgence.
Many in Dhaka remain sceptical that Hasina will actually return, viewing the announcement as a means of galvanising a demoralised party.
Yet the Awami League has achieved something politically: it is back in the conversation. Immediately after Hasina's fall, even mentioning the party was taboo. Now its future is being debated across the political spectrum.
Shafiqul Alam, editor of the English-language daily Daily Waadaa and former press secretary to the Muhammad Yunus-led interim government, believes the party is "exploiting cracks in the unity forged during the uprising".
He told the BBC that "disagreements" over the July Charter, external, proposed constitutional changes and the referendum have "widened divisions" between the elected BNP government and rivals Jamaat-e-Islami and the youth-led National Citizen Party (NCP).
"The Awami League sees an opening," Alam told the BBC. "The party believes this is an opportune moment to take to the streets, exploiting a weakened police force and divisions among the forces of the July uprising."
Analysts say if Hasina returns it could just as easily deepen hostility as revive her party's fortunes. The government has framed the sporadic recent violence as terrorism, while supporters insist their demonstrations are peaceful and accuse the authorities of repression.
The larger question is whether Bangladesh can sustain the exclusion of a political constituency as substantial as the Awami League without creating another source of instability.
For India, the dilemma is increasingly difficult to manage.
Delhi has sheltered Hasina, but her public remarks have angered Dhaka, which wants her extradited. India has sought to repair ties through diplomatic outreach and talks on trade, border security and other bilateral issues, but relations remain strained.
The chill is striking: nearly 10 months into his tenure, Prime Minister Tarique Rahman has yet to visit India.
A trip was reportedly in the offing in August, but Hasina's press conference in Delhi proved a setback to efforts to reset relations.
Avinash Paliwal, who teaches politics and international studies at SOAS University of London, argues that Hasina's latest announcement has "shifted the burden of choice to Dhaka rather than Delhi".
Delhi, he says, "feels it has tried its best" to work with Rahman's government over the past 10 months - "from appointing a political heavyweight as high commissioner, external with cabinet rank to offering fresh talks on security and trade".
"The failure of this outreach has left India disillusioned with Dhaka. India seems to have decided that bilateral relations will likely remain tense whatever it does, so there is little reason to stop Hasina from stirring the political pot."
Delhi has the leverage to restrain Hasina from making political statements on Indian soil, Paliwal argues, but may not want to exercise it.
Nor, in his view, is it in India's interest to see the Awami League permanently excluded from Bangladeshi politics.
"The political party still enjoys pockets of support across Bangladesh and is weaved into the social and political fabric of the country," he says. "So, yes, it is in India's interest, and also in Bangladesh's long-term interests, to rehabilitate the Awami League and take the path of political reconciliation."
That view is increasingly contested in Dhaka.
"There is a perception in Bangladesh that India wants to rehabilitate the Awami League. There are issues India has not resolved, including the extradition of Hasina. India has also not renewed the transit facilities that could benefit Bangladeshi garment exporters, while the Ganges water treaty, external is nearing expiry without much progress. But has India done enough to win back trust?" says Alam.
"For now, only tourist and medical visas have resumed. Everything else remains in limbo."
A Dhaka-based foreign-policy expert, who asked not to be named, says the two countries remain locked in "mutual frustration".
Hasina, he says, remains central to the impasse. "She remains the elephant in the room, but we also have to find a way to move beyond Hasina."
Paliwal argues that the least damaging outcome for India would be Hasina returning to face a fresh trial, with the Awami League rehabilitated under a different operational leadership.
"It will reintroduce a degree of balance in Bangladeshi politics, and will afford India space to protect its long-term interests and equities better," he says.
For now, 16 December is not yet a confirmed journey. But Hasina has already succeeded in making her return a question that neither Dhaka nor Delhi can ignore.
"December could be chaotic. Everyone in Dhaka is on edge," says the foreign-policy expert, warning of protests and confrontation as Hasina's proposed return date approaches - and the possibility that it could be postponed yet again.
"Hasina is unlikely to return, as she would face a death sentence. But her comments have clearly galvanized her supporters," says Pearl Pandya, Acled's South Asia analyst.
But the impasse is also complicating India's ties with Bangladesh. As Paliwal puts it, the "next window of serious negotiations will now open only after Hasina returns to Dhaka, or Dhaka relents under pressure and returns to the table".

noticias.titulo: Met Police ruined my life, says Kenyan man wrongly sentenced over attack on UK couple
noticias.resumen: Evidence from a British police officer helped convict Ali Kololo over a 2011 attack in the Kenyan resort of Lamu.
noticias.texto:
Met Police ruined my life, says Kenyan man wrongly sentenced over attack on UK couple
- Published
A Kenyan woodcutter who was wrongly sentenced to death over an attack on a British couple has told the BBC that actions by London's Metropolitan Police involved in the case destroyed his life.
Somali gunmen broke into David and Judith Tebbutt's beach bungalow on the Kenyan coast in 2011. They shot David dead and abducted Judith, holding her captive in Somalia for six months.
Met detectives flew to Kenya to assist the investigation. Their evidence helped convict Ali Kololo, who spent more than a decade in prison before his conviction was overturned.
Kololo is suing the Met, claiming a senior officer, former Detective Superintendent Neil Hibberd, gave misleading evidence at his trial and acted unlawfully to secure his conviction.
In his first media interview, he told the BBC about his 15-year ordeal and his fight for compensation, which the Met is challenging in court.
We meet on Lamu, a small island off Kenya's northern coast, once a thriving Swahili port. People and goods are still carted through its narrow stone streets by donkey rather than car.
It was here, in 2013, that Kololo was sentenced to death.
Standing at the jetty, where police once brought him ashore in handcuffs, he relishes being free. But he is struggling to rebuild his life.
"Everything was taken from me. I'm starting from zero. I don't think I'll ever go back to who I was before," he says.
Before his arrest, Kololo lived with his wife and their three young children. He had once worked as a groundskeeper at the resort where the Tebbutts were staying, but by 2011 he earned his living felling trees in a local forest and selling the wood.
"My life was very good," he says. "I was fending for myself, taking good care of my family."
Within 24 hours of the attack, Kenyan police had arrested him.
"I was beaten with clubs and thrown into a car," he says. "They beat me for days, burning me with cigarettes, forcing me to confess to things. They subjected me to torture like no other."
Kololo could not read or write. He says police made him put his thumbprint on a statement claiming he had led the attackers to the Tebbutts.
"I didn't understand anything," he says, calling the statement "a mountain of lies". "I signed it without knowing what it was because of the state they had put me in".
The Kenyan police told us it "at all times strives to work within the law". Kololo is not suing them.
Within days of the attack, a team of Met officers, led by then Detective Superintendent Neil Hibberd, arrived to support the Kenyan investigation. The UK government had instructed the officers not to accept information from the Kenyan authorities that had been obtained by interrogating detainees.
But Hibberd requested Kololo's statement and later relied on it when giving evidence for the prosecution at his trial.
In court, Hibberd also presented evidence linking Kololo to the attack. He told the Kenyan court Kololo had been wearing a type of shoe that matched footwear marks found in the sand at the resort.
The officer who had arrested Kololo said he was barefoot when he was handed to police. Hibberd did not disclose that the Met's own forensic examination could not establish whether the shoe in question had made the marks.
At the trial, Kololo did not initially have a lawyer. He had to cross-examine all the prosecution witnesses himself, including Hibberd, through an interpreter who spoke Swahili, which was not Kololo's first language.
"I believe I was framed because I am a poor man and I did not have the strength or means to fight for myself," Kololo says.
Kololo was convicted of kidnap and robbery with violence - the only person ever convicted in connection with the attack. He spent three years on death row before his sentence was commuted to life imprisonment.
He recalls seeing his prison file. In the space for the expiry date, someone had written "death".
"I was completely heartbroken. I believed I could be executed at any moment, and I would never see my family, my children, ever again."
Years later, the UK's Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) established that Hibberd had omitted significant forensic evidence at the trial. It found that he would have had a case to answer for gross misconduct, but he could not face disciplinary proceedings because he had retired from the force. At the time, his lawyer said Hibberd absolutely disagreed with the report's findings.
In April 2023, Kenya's High Court quashed Kololo's conviction, because of doubts over the prosecution's evidence. This followed years of work by the legal charity Reprieve and a Kenyan lawyer, Alfred Olaba, who represented him for free.
They were supported by Judith Tebbutt, who believed Kololo was innocent. In an interview with the BBC in 2022, she said he had been scapegoated by Scotland Yard.
"He was not there on the night. He was not part of the group that held me. They've put this man in prison without any real evidence."
More than three years after his release, Kololo says he is still living with the effects of his torture and decade in prison. As we walk the narrow streets of Lamu's old town, his thin frame moves stiffly. He is on edge. "My mind is not good," he says. "I have not recovered."
He remembers being kept in a filthy, bedbug-ridden cell with up to eight other inmates, which he thought he would never leave. Twice he contracted tuberculosis and nearly died.
Kololo is now too frail to do the woodcutting he once relied on to make a living. He tries to grow enough to eat on the land around his home, but erratic rain makes it difficult.
"I have nothing. On the days I get food, I eat, and on the days I don't, I endure."
He lives alone in a mud hut. His wife divorced him after he went to prison, and their children went to live with his mother. They dropped out of school because the family could not pay the fees. Kololo says they were not allowed to visit him in prison. When he was released, they barely remembered him, especially his youngest.
"They were too young. Only now are they starting to regain the memory that 'this is our father who disappeared'," he says. "If it weren't for my mother, my children might have died."
For much of our time together, Kololo is remarkably upbeat. He trusts that his lawyers and God will deliver him justice. But when we talk about the Met, his demeanour shifts.
"I am extremely angry with the police," he says. "I'm also angry with the Kenyan Police. They collaborated to incriminate me. What [Hibberd] said destroyed my entire life and my children's lives."
The Met has not apologised to Kololo or admitted wrongdoing. The force is contesting his compensation claim, which his lawyers say could take years to resolve.
"These people falsely accused me. Do I not deserve something?" he asks.
The Met told the BBC that neither they nor Hibberd wanted to comment on Kololo's claim, but it said: "Our thoughts are with Mr Kololo, Mrs Tebbutt, her family and all those who have been affected by this terrible crime. The Metropolitan Police remains committed to supporting the Kenyan authorities in any way that may be possible, in order to get justice for Mrs Tebbutt and her late husband."
Preetha Gopalan, Reprieve's head of UK litigation, describes the Met's behaviour in Kololo's case as "egregious".
"They've spent 10 years trying to evade accountability in every way possible, now dragging him through the courts," she says. "It's possible for them to do the right thing, but they are unwilling, and so this ordeal continues to haunt Kololo and his family."
"Even if I get a billion shillings, I will never be the same," Kololo says. "But if I get the justice I deserve, I can help my children and take care of myself when I am an old man."

noticias.titulo: Zelenskyy warns of major Russian attack as Trump urges Putin to ‘pull back’
noticias.resumen: Trump says he urged Putin to 'pull back' military aggression in Europe amid escalating Russian and Ukrainian attacks.
noticias.texto:
Zelenskyy warns of major Russian attack as Trump urges Putin to ‘pull back’
Trump says he urged Putin to ‘pull back’ military aggression in Europe amid escalating Russian and Ukrainian attacks.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says Ukraine has information that Russia is preparing a new mass strike on the country in the coming days.
“Unfortunately, we have information about a new mass strike being prepared by the Russians,” he said in his nightly video address on Thursday. “In the coming days, please pay attention to the alarms of missile threats.”
It was the second such warning from Zelenskyy this week. He also had a message for Moscow: “We will rebuild what is ours and retaliate against every Russian strike.”
Trump urges Putin to pull back
US President Donald Trump said he had pressed Russian President Vladimir Putin to ease Russia’s military actions in Europe.
In a post on Truth Social, Trump said he spent “a lot of time” in talks with Putin in China on the issue of Putin pulling back “all Military aggression against territories throughout Europe”.
“Thousands of people are being killed each and every month, A COMPLETE BLOODBATH,” Trump wrote. He said he hoped that would allow a deal between Russia and Ukraine to be “made quickly”, which he called “a strong possibility”.
Trump said he updated NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte on the talks during a meeting at his Mar-a-Lago club in Florida on Wednesday night.
Latest attacks
Russia struck Kyiv with ballistic missiles overnight, wounding seven people and hitting a shopping centre and two other buildings, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
Moscow said it hit drone-related sites in the city. Russian forces have attacked Kyiv and other cities almost continuously since September.
Ukraine said its drones hit an oil refinery in Russia’s southern Krasnodar region, oil reservoirs at a Transneft facility in Bashkortostan and the Marinovka military airfield in the Volgograd region.
Ukraine has also widened its attacks at sea. On Monday, Zelenskyy said Ukraine used seven naval drones to hit the Russian corvette Merkury and the cargo ship Angara off Libya. Libyan officials told the Associated Press news agency that the Merkury was heavily damaged but not sunk.
At about the same time, a suspected Ukrainian drone struck the Russia-bound cargo ship Sparta II in the Baltic Sea, near Finland. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov called the attacks a “very dangerous trend“.
At least four Russian vessels have been targeted this month.
Europe’s funding for Ukraine
European Union leaders are struggling at a summit in Brussels to agree on a new 45 billion euro ($49bn) loan to help Ukraine meet its economic and military needs next year. It would come on top of a 90 billion euro ($99bn) loan, agreed nearly a year ago, that covers most of Ukraine’s government needs for 2026 and 2027.
Early on Friday in Brussels, European Council President Antonio Costa said that 24 member states supported the new loan, as talks on the bloc’s next seven-year budget stretched on.
The loan is tangled up with the EU’s budget for 2028 to 2034, which includes about $110bn for Ukraine over seven years. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has threatened to hold up the budget unless all member states make a “collective commitment” to Ukraine.
North Korea ‘pauses’ arms deliveries
Ukraine’s military intelligence agency (GUR) said on Thursday that North Korea has temporarily halted some military cooperation with Russia after diplomatic tensions between the allies.
It said this includes deliveries of KN-23 ballistic missiles and artillery shells, and Russian military flights over North Korean territory.
GUR said North Korea’s Foreign Minister Choe Son-hui announced the pause last month in response to a Russian deputy foreign minister’s assertion that Moscow would help ease tensions between Seoul and Pyongyang.
GUR also said Pyongyang is holding off on a Russian request to raise North Korea’s military presence in Russia from about 8,500 to 50,000 troops.
It added that North Korean units remain in Russia’s Kursk region and that a North Korean missile unit has been in the Voronezh region since mid-summer, from where Russia strikes Ukraine.
South Korean and Western intelligence agencies have said Pyongyang sent more than 10,000 soldiers to Russia’s Kursk region in 2024, along with artillery shells, missiles and long-range rocket systems.
Strikes continue
On November 20, Russia fired more than 400 drones and 110 missiles at Ukraine, killing eight people, Zelenskyy said.
It was one of the largest attacks of the war and followed Putin’s vow to retaliate for Ukrainian strikes on the Kerch Bridge linking Russia to Crimea.

noticias.titulo: Global news agency AFP reports cyberattack, shuts down content platform
noticias.resumen: France's cybersecurity chief urges collective action to combat unprecedented threat levels in the nation.
noticias.texto:
Global news agency AFP reports cyberattack, shuts down content platform
France’s cybersecurity chief urges collective action to combat unprecedented threat levels in the nation.
Agence France-Presse (AFP) has been hit by a cyberattack, requiring the AFP Forum content platform to be taken offline.
The France-based international news agency’s management said on Thursday that it is currently investigating the circumstances of the cyberattack, including who was behind it.
“AFP was hit by a cyber attack overnight, starting at 1:30 am (Paris time) [00:30 GMT]. The target was AFP Forum, one of the platforms our clients use to browse and download our content,” an internal email from AFP management said.
“As soon as the intrusion was detected, our teams moved immediately to contain the intrusion and took AFP Forum offline as a precautionary measure. AFP Forum remains unavailable until further notice.”
AFP is reportedly offering backup solutions to the agency’s subscribers while the portal is offline.
France’s cybersecurity chief, Vincent Strubel, warned on Thursday that the country faces an unprecedented level of cybersecurity threats and called for collective efforts to strengthen defences against attacks.
“We are facing a level of threat that is unprecedented, with an intensity we have never experienced before,” Strubel said in an interview with France Inter radio.
The incident is the latest in a slew of cybersecurity disruptions across European countries. FIFA, which is based in Zurich, Switzerland, confirmed to Al Jazeera on Thursday that it had been the victim of a cyberattack that gave unauthorised access to personal and business information.
In October, several French supermarkets were hit by an “unprecedented” cyberattack that raised the temperature of fridges and freezers to as high as 50 degrees Celsius (122F).
Temperature spikes were also recorded in stores in 10 other European countries in early November, including the United Kingdom, Germany, Belgium and Sweden.
France accused Tehran of being behind the October attack and summoned Iran’s ambassador to Paris to “lodge a very strong protest”.
Iran called Paris’s accusations “baseless” and condemned the “hackneyed policy of levelling accusations against the Islamic republic”.

noticias.titulo: Argentina bars Central Bank from printing money to fund government spending
noticias.resumen: The South American country's Senate also advances proposal to suspend primary elections ahead of 2027 presidential race.
noticias.texto:
Argentina bars Central Bank from printing money to fund government spending
The South American country’s Senate also advanced a proposal to suspend primary elections ahead of the 2027 presidential race.
Argentina’s legislature has pushed forward a series of bills that would implement changes sought by President Javier Milei, including barring the Central Bank from printing extra money for government expenses.
On Thursday, the Argentinian Chamber of Deputies gave final approval to a bill imposing restrictions on the Central Bank, defining its “primary and fundamental mission” as maintaining the value of the country’s currency.
Under past administrations, the Central Bank has printed additional funds to help cover government expenses, contributing to the country’s once sky-high inflation, which reached more than 200 percent in 2023.
Milei, a libertarian economist, swept into office that year on a promise to tame runaway inflation and slash government spending.
Under his leadership, inflation has declined, though poverty has surged. Economists also believe Argentina may be drifting into a recession, with economic activity diminished in recent months.
Still, Milei’s office celebrated the Senate’s passage of the Central Bank bill with a presidential statement.
“This marks the end of nearly two decades of political manipulation at the Central Bank,” the statement said.
The bank, founded in 1935, had experienced “91 years of plunder, expropriation, impunity, and institutional decay” up to this point, it added.
The vote in the Chamber of Deputies was 141 to zero, with 99 abstentions.
The Senate previously passed the bill, though it removed language Milei had pressed for, which would have required a two-thirds vote in both chambers of Congress to remove Central Bank governors.
Bill seeks to suspend primary elections
Also on Thursday, Argentina’s Senate advanced a bill to reform the country’s elections by suspending its primaries.
Unlike the Central Bank reform, that bill was not final. It still needs to pass the Chamber of Deputies.
The bill, however, comes less than a year before Argentina is slated to hold its next presidential election. Milei is expected to seek re-election in the October 24 vote.
Critics see the suspension of primaries as a means for Milei to avoid early pushback in his campaign.
A dismal primary result, they say, could weaken his momentum ahead of the general election and cause unfavourable economic fluctuations. Milei has long faced public discontent over his programme of economic austerity.
Thursday’s bill would also reduce public financing for political parties and eliminate a mandatory presidential debate ahead of general elections.
Senators approved the legislation by a vote of 43 to 29. While members of Milei’s La Libertad Avanza party touted the bill as a means of simplifying Argentina’s elections, opponents warned it could erode democratic norms.
“Milei now wants to change the rules of democracy to improve his chances of reelection by cheating,” Buenos Aires province Governor Axel Kicillof, a potential challenger to Milei, said in a social media post.

noticias.titulo: Georgian police clash with Turkiye’s Besiktas fans over Palestinian flag
noticias.resumen: Match between Besiktas and Hapoel Beer-Sheva suspended for 30 minutes after confrontation between fans and police.
noticias.texto:
Georgian police clash with Turkiye’s Besiktas fans over Palestinian flag
Match between Besiktas and Hapoel Beer-Sheva suspended for 30 minutes after confrontation between fans and police in Georgia.
Georgian police have clashed with fans of Turkiye’s Besiktas after they unfurled a Palestinian flag during a Europa League game against Israel’s Hapoel Beer-Sheva.
The clashes resulted in a suspension of about 30 minutes during the 26th minute of the game held in Batumi, Georgia, but it resumed after the interruption on Thursday. Besiktas eventually won 2-1.
Turkish media outlets reported that Georgian police entered the stands and used pepper spray against fans of the Istanbul giant, prompting Danish referee Morten Krogh to stop the game with the score 0-0.
The game was relocated by UEFA to Batumi after Turkish authorities said Istanbul could not host it for safety and security reasons. Unlike two previous Hapoel away games, spectators were allowed in the stadium.
Besiktas accused Georgian police of using “disproportionate” force against supporters before and during the game.
“We strongly condemn the security forces for their use of disproportionate force against our fans,” the Turkish club said in a statement. “We also extend our best wishes for a speedy recovery to all our fans affected by these incidents.”
The Turkish Football Federation also strongly condemned the treatment of Besiktas supporters, saying they were subjected to unacceptable behaviour and discrimination in a statement on X. The federation said it would press for an investigation into the incident.
Several other Turkish Super Lig clubs, including Trabzonspor, Fenerbahce, Galatasaray, Erzurumspor, Basaksehir and Samsunspor, condemned the use of force against Besiktas fans.
Prior to the match, Besiktas players refused to shake hands with their Hapoel counterparts, Turkiye’s state-run Anadolu Agency reported.
A video published by Besiktas on X after the game shows their players posing for a picture behind fans carrying a banner that reads: “Rise up against the occupation. Freedom for Palestine.”
Diplomatic incident
Turkish Interior Minister Mustafa Ciftci spoke to his Georgian counterpart following the game to discuss Turkiye’s concern over the incident.
According to Turkiye’s Interior Ministry, Ciftci expressed concern over the disproportionate use of force against Turkish fans and called for measures to ensure their safe return to Turkiye.
Georgian Interior Minister Sulkhan Tamazashvili reportedly said that UEFA officials had confiscated the fans’ Palestinian flags and that Georgian state authorities had played no role in the confiscation.

noticias.titulo: Israeli settlers damage Palestinian family’s homes in West Bank attack
noticias.resumen: The Tubasi family was forced out months ago and has been denied a return by settlers despite an Israeli court order.
noticias.texto:
Israeli settlers damage Palestinian family’s homes in West Bank attack
The Tubasi family was forced out months ago and has been denied a return by settlers despite an Israeli court order.
Israeli settlers have smashed the foundations of two homes belonging to a Palestinian family in the occupied West Bank after attacks stopped the family from returning.
Security cameras showed the settlers bringing a bulldozer to the two-storey houses in the village of Jaloud, near Nablus, at about 1am on Thursday (23:00 GMT on Wednesday), before starting to damage them, Reuters reported. It added that the concrete foundations of the homes had been partially broken.
“This latest escalation is a direct consequence of the lack of law enforcement and the sense of impunity enjoyed by the perpetrators,” said Ghiath Nasser, the owners’ lawyer.
The Israeli military said the attack was “a serious criminal act” and said it was investigating, despite settlers remaining in the vicinity throughout the day.
A family forced out
The Tubasi family now live in a small house in Jaloud with a direct view of the homes they fled. “They want to demolish the houses so that we cannot return to them,” Wael Tubasi, one of the owners, said.
He said the deadline for the military to remove the settlers had passed.
“Even though there is a court order, and the army is required to remove them from the area entirely, not just return us to our homes, it’s still not being implemented,” he said.
The family said settlers set up a tent near their homes in April and began attacking them. They said settlers set fire to the homes, cut their water and electricity and blocked the roads.
After three months, settlers told the family they had an hour to leave or be killed “like the Dawabsheh family”, Wael’s mother, Aedah, said. In 2015, settlers set fire to the Dawabsheh family’s home in the village of Duma, killing an 18-month-old child and both his parents.
In September, soldiers escorted the family back to their homes under the court order. Ten minutes later, about 200 settlers attacked them, forcing the family and the soldiers to retreat, the family said. The settlers then burned the homes and broke much of the furniture.
“I’m forbidden from reaching my home, while the settlers have the right to remain inside. What rights are there?” Aedah said.
Surge in settler pogroms
The attack follows weeks of settler pogroms across the occupied West Bank. There have been an average of 53 settler attacks a week since the start of the year, according to the UN. The agency said on November 20 that more than 400 settler attacks causing casualties or damage had been recorded since September, more than in any previous season.
Over the weekend, settlers set fire to at least a dozen vehicles and several homes in five villages, and sprayed “Revenge” on walls. Last week, settlers killed an elderly Palestinian woman and wounded 10 other people in a pogrom near Jericho.
Very few cases lead to charges.
According to the Israeli rights group Yesh Din, 93.6 percent of investigations into settler pogroms are closed without indictments.

noticias.titulo: In Canada, Quebec’s religious symbols ban faces a Supreme Court test
noticias.resumen: Canada’s top court weighs Bill 21, the Quebec law that shapes where Muslim women can work and where they feel welcome.
noticias.texto:
In Canada, Quebec’s religious symbols ban faces a Supreme Court test
Canada’s top court weighs Bill 21, the Quebec law that shapes where Muslim women can work and where they feel welcome.
Navien Waly had been volunteering at her kids’ schools, helping out at bake sales and serving on graduation committees, for a decade when she received an email informing her that her presence was no longer welcome.
Under Quebec law, it said, parents who wore religious symbols could no longer volunteer.
Waly had started wearing the hijab four years earlier, at age 40.
She said the email felt like a “slap in the face” and that she struggled to respond when her two younger kids, who had got used to their mother’s presence at school, asked what she had done wrong.
“I’m the same person I was 10 years ago,” she said. “It doesn’t make me any different. I’ve never spoken about my religion.”
The law also upended her plans to return to work. Waly, now 45, had left a career in finance to pursue a career as a specialised educator. She was supposed to start work next year, but now, she says she can’t do the work she was trained for as long as she continues to wear the hijab.
The law behind the email, Bill 94, expanded the restrictions that Quebec first introduced under Bill 21 in 2019. On Friday, Canada’s Supreme Court is set to rule on a challenge to that earlier law, which bans public school teachers, police officers and certain other public officials from wearing religious symbols on the job.
The landmark ruling could also clarify how far governments can go in using a provision of Canada’s Charter of Rights and Freedoms to shield laws from certain rights challenges.
‘Your livelihood or your most deeply held convictions’
In the seven years since Bill 21 passed, its impacts have been felt across religious minorities but have been particularly devastating for Muslim women.
In a survey conducted in 2022 and 2023 for a report by the National Council of Canadian Muslims (NCCM) and York University researcher Nadia Hasan, 73 percent of the 411 Muslim women surveyed said Bill 21 had impacted their job search, while 48 percent believed they didn’t get a job because of their religious identity.
Some women take their hijabs off when they get to work and put them back on when they leave, said National Council of Canadian Muslims chief executive Stephen Brown, adding that he’d spoken to women who described the routine as humiliating.
Being made to choose between “your livelihood or your most deeply held convictions”, Brown said, “was a dehumanising and cruel situation to inflict on people”.
But the consequences of the law extend beyond work. In the same survey, 88 percent of Muslim women said the law had made Quebec a less welcoming place to live.
Brown said some Muslims in Quebec had compared the climate to what they see in France, where it’s “open season on Muslims”.
Waly, who was born and raised in Canada, said in recent years, in the period coinciding with Quebec’s policies on religious symbols and her starting to wear the hijab, “things have happened to me that have never happened before”.
A couple of months ago, she was at a grocery store checkout when a man behind her started singing about how immigrants had ruined his life. He sang that he’d lost his job and been forced to retire at age 30 because of “people like you”. Waly turned around and asked in French if he was talking to her. The man went red, she recalled.
In recent years, she’s encountered more hostile looks and racist comments, with strangers telling her: “Go back to your home.”
“What home? This is my home.”
Brown said many Muslim Quebecers who speak English and who can take their work elsewhere have left the province or are planning to. For those who only speak French, relocating can be much harder, he said.
People have suggested to Waly that she move to another province, too. But she can’t imagine leaving her family and the place where she grew up. Her father, brothers, nieces and nephews all live in Quebec.
“You can’t, after living here for 45 years, to just uproot your whole life.”
How Bill 21 came to be
When Quebec introduced Bill 21 in 2019, the government presented it as a moderate approach to settling the province’s long-running debate over secularism.
The debate goes back to the 1960s Quiet Revolution when Quebec began taking control of public institutions like schools and hospitals away from the Catholic Church.
Decades later, tensions over how those institutions should accommodate religious minorities led to the Bouchard-Taylor commission. The commission recommended that judges, police and others who exercise the coercive power of the state be barred from wearing religious symbols at work.
With Bill 21, the Coalition Avenir Quebec government took things further, bringing public school teachers under the ban. Those who were already in their posts could keep wearing religious symbols as long as they didn’t change jobs or employers.
In an interview with Radio-Canada days after the law passed, Premier Francois Legault defended it, saying the majority had felt ignored on the issue for years. “To avoid extremes, you have to give a bit to the majority,” he said, suggesting the far right would want to take things even further, and stressing that religious symbols could still be worn in the street.
Polling ahead of the law passing found that 64 percent of respondents in Quebec supported the bill.
In Brown’s view, the legislation, which was put together during an election campaign, was about getting votes, tapping into longstanding distrust of organised religion, anti-Muslim sentiment and fears about the future of Quebec’s French-speaking culture.
“You combine those together, and it becomes a really effective wedge when it comes to driving support towards the party during elections,” he said.
In the years since, Quebec has expanded the restrictions beyond the jobs covered by Bill 21.
In 2025, Bill 94 extended the ban on religious symbols to school support staff and volunteers, including parents like Waly. It also required students to keep their faces uncovered at school and barred prayer on school premises.
And earlier this year, Bill 9 extended the symbols ban to include daycare staff, forbade face coverings at Quebec’s public colleges and universities, and restricted where people could pray on campus.
The newly elected Parti Quebecois government has now pledged to ban elementary school students from wearing religious symbols in schools.
What’s at stake in the Supreme Court ruling?
When Quebec passed Bill 21, it used a provision known as the notwithstanding clause, which lets governments keep a law in place even if it violates certain rights protected by Canada’s Charter of Rights and Freedoms, including freedom of religion and the right to equality. That protection lasts up to five years at a time and can be renewed. Quebec renewed it in 2024, saying it was needed to preserve “social peace”.
A Quebec court found in 2021 that the law infringed on the rights of people who wear religious symbols, but upheld most of the law because Quebec had invoked the notwithstanding clause. The Quebec Court of Appeal upheld the ruling in 2024 and reversed an exemption for English-language school boards. The Supreme Court heard the case in March.
The NCCM, the Canadian Civil Liberties Association, the World Sikh Organization and others are challenging the law. They argue it violates constitutional rights despite Quebec’s use of the notwithstanding clause.
Brown said the council wants the court to invalidate the use of the clause in this case.
“The notwithstanding clause is supposed to be an extraordinary power of last resort,” he said, arguing it should not be used in cases where “governments are deliberately targeting the rights of citizens for political gain”.
Waly is not optimistic that the court will overturn the law, but is holding out hope that she won’t have to start over.
“At 45 years old, to start thinking of another path? I don’t know what I’m going to do,” she said. “Something’s gotta give.”
But she worries about her kids, who are now grappling with what the restrictions could mean for their future. Her oldest daughter had talked about wearing the hijab one day, but now she’s weighing it against jobs that she may want to do.
“‘Either I give up on all these different positions that I can’t do or I don’t wear the hijab,’” she recalled her daughter telling her.
“And it’s just kind of up in the air,” said Waly. “I don’t have an answer for that.”

noticias.titulo: Report: CIA tortured more people with waterboarding than US agency admitted
noticias.resumen: A New York Times report lends credence to long-held belief that torture method was more widely used than acknowledged.
noticias.texto:
Report: CIA tortured more people with waterboarding than US agency admitted
A New York Times report lends credence to the long-held belief that the torture method was more widely used than acknowledged.
The New York Times has reported that the United States Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) may have waterboarded more people than it previously admitted.
Wednesday’s report comes after the newspaper filed a lawsuit to obtain material gathered by special prosecutor John Durham, who was appointed in 2008 to investigate the CIA’s activities.
Durham’s probe ended without any criminal charges. But The New York Times obtained partially redacted documents from his investigation, including a summary of a 2012 interview with an interpreter who described a previously unconfirmed act of waterboarding.
The account sheds new light on one of the most infamous methods of torture utilised by the intelligence agency after the attacks on September 11, 2001.
Waterboarding involves restraining a person and pouring water on their face through a cloth, to mimic the experience of drowning.
The CIA called the practice an “enhanced interrogation technique”. As part of the US’s so-called “war on terror”, the agency sent suspects to overseas prisons, known as black sites, where they would be tortured in secret, including through waterboarding.
While the practice was shielded from scrutiny for years, a 2009 executive order eventually barred continued waterboarding. Congress has likewise passed restrictions.
But rights groups have long suspected that such abuses were much more widespread than the CIA admitted. The agency had previously acknowledged waterboarding three detainees.
According to the documents The New York Times received, a contract translator who worked with the CIA observed an additional case of waterboarding.
While the documents do not specify where the translator worked, the newspaper said it determined that the location was likely a black site outside of Bagram Air Force Base on the outskirts of Kabul, Afghanistan.
The translator, The New York Times explained, referenced a detainee death that matched a facility known as Detention Site Cobalt or the “Salt Pit”, which became infamous for abusive conditions.
In an interview with the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), the translator stated that he had seen a man referred to as “Bashir” facing the torture practice.
He described Bahir as “lying on the board with the head of the board tilted downward into the water”.
“There were approximately three to four people ‘doing this,’” the document said, summarising the translator’s statements.
The FBI summary explains that the translator “saw the incident in passing but did not participate himself”. The incident allegedly took place in a hallway.
The CIA did not respond to Al Jazeera’s request for comment by the time of this article’s publication.
The agency has also not acknowledged waterboarding detainees at any site in Afghanistan. The three detainees it has acknowledged torturing were held at black sites in Thailand and Poland.
One was Abu Zubaydah, the first detainee the CIA held in a black-site prison, located in Thailand. The US government for years falsely depicted him as one of the highest-ranking members of al-Qaeda, a group of which he was not a member, according to US intelligence reports.
A 2014 report on the CIA torture programme by the Senate Intelligence Committee found that Zubaydah was waterboarded 83 times, sometimes as a means of helping instruct torture methods.
Another was Khalid Shaikh Mohammed, accused of being the architect of the September 11 attacks.
The third was Abd al-Rahim al-Nashiri, who is accused of helping plan al-Qaeda’s 2000 bombing of a Navy destroyer, the USS Cole.
All three are currently being held in the Guantanamo Bay military prison in Cuba.

noticias.titulo: Egypt detains driver over Cairo fuel tanker fire that killed 31
noticias.resumen: Prosecutors order drug tests for the 21-year-old suspect, who says he was overtaking when the crash happened.
noticias.texto:
Egypt detains driver over Cairo fuel tanker fire that killed 31
Prosecutors order drug tests for the 21-year-old suspect, who says he was overtaking when the crash happened.
Prosecutors in Egypt have ordered the detention of a 21-year-old driver suspected of causing a collision on Wednesday that overturned a fuel tanker on Cairo’s ring road, starting a fire that killed 31 people.
The Public Prosecution announced on Thursday that it had ordered the man to be held pending an investigation, and sent him to the Forensic Medicine Authority for tests to determine whether he had taken drugs.
The tanker burst into flames at about 6:30pm (16:30 GMT) on Wednesday, at the height of the evening rush hour, on an elevated stretch of the ring road in al-Waraq, a densely populated district of Giza on the western edge of the capital. The fire spread to passing traffic and destroyed 27 vehicles, including cars and motorcycles.
In an earlier statement, prosecutors said the driver told investigators he had been travelling from al-Marg towards al-Haram at 110km/h (68mph), with his father in the car, and was switching lanes to overtake other vehicles when the front left of his car struck the rear right of the tanker.
The man told prosecutors he then lost control and his car veered to the far right of the road. One of the tanker’s tyres burst, the statement said, before the vehicle hit a concrete barrier and overturned. Petrol leaking from the truck caught fire.
Identifying remains
Prosecutors said they identified the driver after inspecting the scene and interviewing witnesses, and had since spoken to all the injured whose condition allowed them to be questioned. Forensic teams are taking DNA samples from victims’ relatives to identify some of the bodies. Relatives posted appeals on Facebook for men who had been on the road and had not been heard from since, the Reuters news agency reported.
The investigation will determine whether the driver bears criminal responsibility.
The Ministry of Health and Population on Thursday put the final toll at 31 dead and 26 injured, up from the 21 injured it had reported on Wednesday. Five of the injured have left hospital. The other 21 are still being treated, including eight transferred to other hospitals for further care. The bodies of the dead are in the custody of prosecutors, the ministry said.
By Thursday morning, traffic was moving again after crews cleared most of the burned wreckage. Salah Ahmed, a microbus driver, told the AP news agency that he had been on the ring road when the tanker caught fire but was held back by traffic, which saved his life.
“It was God’s hellfire on the ring road,” he said. “Why is a truck like this on the ring road at a rush hour? Who gets penalised for this happening?”
A 2018 cabinet decision barred trucks carrying more than four tonnes from the ring road between 6am and midnight, the AFP news agency reported. Prosecutors have not said why the tanker was on the road at the time.
“The tanks were exploding, the tyres were exploding, and there was fire,” Zaghlol al-Me, a local resident who reached the scene shortly after the crash, told Reuters. “We just didn’t know what to do or how to save anyone.”
Government pledges support for victims
The Public Prosecution’s statements are the first official account of how the crash happened. Early reports in local media suggested that a high-voltage cable had fallen in front of the tanker. On Wednesday night, the Ministry of Transport denied issuing any statement to that effect and said the cause was a matter for prosecutors.
The Ministry of Electricity and Renewable Energy said the overhead lines were taut when the fire began and that two circuits tripped only after it started. The ministry’s spokesman, Mansour Abdel Ghani, told the Egyptian Youm7 daily newspaper that the lines had no connection to the crash and melted in the heat. A high-voltage line lay twisted on the ground on Thursday, AP reported.
President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi ordered full medical care for the injured and support for the families of those killed. Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly visited the injured on Thursday with Health Minister Khaled Abdel Ghaffar and Social Solidarity Minister Maya Morsy. Madbouly said the government, civil society and businesspeople would provide bank investment certificates to give bereaved families a stable income, and replacement vehicles for people whose cars burned.
“We realise that no compensation or money can make up for those we have lost,” Madbouly said.
Egypt’s Ministry of Social Solidarity said on Thursday that people could donate through the InstaPay app to help the injured and the families of those killed. It also opened an account at Nasser Social Bank for donations from businesses and civil society groups. The cabinet said the ministry had received 24 million Egyptian pounds (about $445,000) from seven charities.
Calls for accountability
The crash has renewed questions about road safety in Egypt. The Ministry of Transport says it spent about $37bn on transport between 2014 and 2024, yet 5,829 people were killed on the country’s roads in 2025, up 10.8 percent from the year before, and about 84,000 were injured, according to the state statistics agency, CAPMAS.
Egyptian legislators demanded accountability on Thursday. Mahmoud Samy, an MP, said the government needed to move from “building roads and expanding them to managing their safety professionally”. Abdel Moneim Imam, a politician who chairs the liberal Justice Party, said the cabinet bore full responsibility and should resign.
Amr Moussa, Egypt’s former foreign minister and former secretary-general of the Arab League, also criticised what he described as a deterioration in government oversight.
“Trading accusations and evading responsibility leads to the next disaster,” Moussa said, according to Reuters.
Transport Minister Kamel al-Wazir was appointed in 2019 after a train crash at Cairo’s Ramses station triggered a fire that killed 25 people, according to Reuters. He has rejected calls to resign since then, including after a lorry crash in the Nile Delta that killed 19 people, almost all of them young women, last year. The ministry declined to comment further when contacted by Reuters.
Earlier this month, a train crash, also in Giza, killed at least seven people and injured more than 125, prompting calls from legislators for accountability over recurring transport accidents.

Attack on Saudi’s Jazan refinery kills one person, disrupts operations
The attack killed a Nepali national, injured several people and sparked a fire, Saudi Energy Ministry says.
An aerial projectile has hit an oil refinery in Saudi Arabia’s city of Jazan, killing one worker and injuring several other people, according to the country’s Ministry of Energy.
Thursday’s attack on the facility on the kingdom’s Red Sea coast caused a fire and temporarily halted some operations, the ministry said.
The statement did not identify who carried out the strike, but earlier the Saudi-led military coalition fighting Yemen’s Houthis said that the Iranian-backed group had attacked the refinery. It came after Saudi Arabia’s civil defence agency had issued an alert about potential danger in Jazan province.
The strike was the Houthis‘ latest blow against key Saudi facilities, a day after the group claimed attacks on Ras Tanura, the kingdom’s largest refinery and a major crude export hub, and the Red Sea ports of Jeddah and Jazan, amid escalating hostilities between the two sides.
The Saudi Ministry of Energy said the worker who died was Nepali, while the injured were of various nationalities.
The injured received medical care, while emergency personnel and specialised technical teams arrived at the site to assess the damage and verify the safety of the facilities following the attack, the ministry added.
The refinery in southwestern Saudi Arabia, near the Yemeni border, is designed to process up to 400,000 barrels of crude oil per day.
The Saudi-led coalition, which is backing Yemen’s internationally recognised government in its fight with the Houthis, condemned the strike and threatened a counterattack.
“Targeting civilians and civilian infrastructure would be met with a firm military ‌‌response,” coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki posted on X.
Later on Thursday, the coalition claimed its forces had destroyed a Houthi ballistic missile launch platform in Yemen’s Hodeidah governorate used by the armed group to stage the attack on the Jazan refinery, according to al-Maliki. There was no immediate statement from the Houthis regarding the strike.
Fighting in Yemen
On the ground in Yemen, meanwhile, Saudi-backed government forces claimed they had carried out 767 strikes on Houthi positions on Thursday.
In a post on X, the forces’ spokesman Majed Abdullah al-Nuzaili said the strikes had “neutralised” 117 Houthi fighters and destroyed 87 vehicles and combat assets.
Al-Nuzaili added that government forces continued to confront Houthi formations on the front lines in northern and western Marib governorate, as well as in the governorates of al-Jawf, Taiz, Lahj, Shabwah and Hajjah.
Earlier on Thursday, a series of air strikes targeted Yemen’s Houthi-held capital, Sanaa, according to media affiliated with the armed group, which is also known as Ansar Allah – Arabic for Supporters of God.
Elsewhere, Houthi forces targeted Habib al-Sarm and al-Hujalla, as well as al-Aqroud in al-Masrakh district.
The Houthis, who control the most populous areas of Yemen, have launched missiles and drones at Saudi airports, oil facilities and office buildings since the country’s civil war reignited in July, in a spillover from the US-Iran war.
The attacks have previously temporarily disrupted some of Aramco’s operations and caused the cancellation of most international flights to Riyadh. They also forced Saudi Arabia to postpone or cancel major international events, including football’s AFC Asian Cup and the flagship FII investment conference.
The fighting has also exacerbated dire humanitarian conditions for Yemeni civilians.
The World Health Organization (WHO) reported that as of Monday, 2,361 people had been killed and 10,982 injured since fighting in Yemen escalated in August. More than 360,000 people have also been forced to flee their homes in Yemen since the start of August, according to the UN.

noticias.titulo: Mexico seeks US talks about suspected SpaceX debris
noticias.resumen: Mexico concerned as SpaceX ramps up rocket launches from Starbase near border in Texas.
noticias.texto:
Mexico seeks US talks about suspected SpaceX debris
Mexico concerned as SpaceX ramps up rocket launches from Starbase near border in Texas.
The Mexican government is seeking talks with aviation authorities in the United States about falling rocket debris following SpaceX launches in Texas.
It is the latest sign of growing tensions between Mexico City and Elon Musk’s trillion-dollar company.
“What we are seeking, through the embassy, is a meeting between US and Mexican airspace authorities so that permission for the use of Mexican airspace can be established, how often it would be used, and, if necessary, the relocation of the launch site,” Mexico’s President Claudia Sheinbaum said on Thursday at a news conference in the capital.
“And then there’s the issue of the debris,” she added.
Earlier this month, Mexican authorities said they had to recover debris after a launch of a SpaceX Starship from its Starbase,Texas, facility near the Gulf of Mexico and nature reserves on both sides of the shared border.
Debris that officials said came from the launch washed ashore along Playa Bagdad in Matamoros in the Mexican state of Tamaulipas, according to PROFEPA, Mexico’s Federal Attorney for Environmental Protection.
It said it had collected material several days after part of the Starship was destroyed and fell into the sea. The debris was taken by the Mexican navy to be stored and PROFEPA said it would ask SpaceX to take possession of it.
SpaceX said it was working with Mexican authorities and disputed the claim that what was found was from its failed Starship launch.
“We continue to stay in contact with the Mexican government and are on standby to send support if authorities in Mexico tell us it is actually needed,” the company posted on X. “Partners on the ground relayed that they have found very little debris in their sweeps of the beach and the small amount they have found is not clearly from SpaceX operations.”
Musk’s SpaceX is seeking permission from the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to dramatically increase activity at the Starbase facility. Previously, the company was allowed 25 launches and 50 landings a year, but now it is seeking permission for 456 launches and 912 landings annually.
Earlier this week, the US Federal Communications Commission granted SpaceX permission to send up to one million satellites into space as part of Musk’s plans to develop data centres in orbit.

noticias.titulo: Musk pledges two SpaceX shares for every US child
noticias.resumen: US children would receive one share from SpaceX and one from him personally, Musk said.
noticias.texto:
Musk pledges two SpaceX shares for every US child
US children would receive one share from SpaceX and one from him personally, Musk said.
Elon Musk plans to gift every child in the United States two SpaceX shares, as he attempts to build public support for his satellite and artifical intelligence businesses during a period of intense public and political scrutiny of the technology sector.
The world’s richest person announced the share giveaway, which is worth a total of about $18bn, on Wednesday evening just hours after SpaceX won US approval to deploy 1 million satellites for data centres in space.
Musk is seeking to expand SpaceX’s role in the AI industry, even as the rapid growth of computing infrastructure raises concern about its environmental impact and the economic and political influence of technology billionaires.
Opponents of data centre development were among the biggest winners for the Democrats in this month’s US midterm elections.
“The initiative clearly helps broaden public participation in the SpaceX story,” Chez Anbu, head of wealth advisory at OCBC in Singapore, said on Thursday.
“Giving children a direct economic stake in the company creates a powerful narrative around broader participation in the benefits of the AI and space economy,” Anbu added.
The Federal Communications Commission said it approved SpaceX’s satellite constellation proposal to help meet rapidly growing demand for AI computing.
Astronomers have long been concerned about such developments in space, and the American Astronomical Society said it was “disheartened and dismayed” by the FCC’s decision.
It warned the proposed constellation would “significantly undermine decades of federal investment in astronomical facilities” and the ability of astronomers and the public to enjoy and study the night sky.
Share giveaway
Children would receive one share from SpaceX and one from him personally, Musk said in a brief post on X.
In a separate post, Musk said the SpaceX company shares would be transferred next month.
“The share directly from me will be transferred when my lockup expires in June next year,” Musk added.
SpaceX said earlier on Wednesday it would contribute one newly issued share of its Class A common stock to every currently active Trump Account, adding that Musk would personally match the number of shares donated by the company.
A Trump Account is a programme designed to give Americans under the age of 18 a stake in the stock market and help build wealth from an early age. The White House said in October it had opened almost 70 million accounts. SpaceX shares closed at $127.44 on Wednesday, valuing the pledge at nearly $18bn.
SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment on whether Musk’s SpaceX share donations would be linked to Trump Accounts.
“What it does is build a massive, long-term retail shareholder base,” said Christopher Brankin, global markets adviser at brokerage Mitrade Group.
“It builds immediate market engagement and creates a massive, financially literate client pipeline for trading platforms as that generation comes of age,” he added.
Musk, whose net worth is approximately $824bn, said last month he would give one of his SpaceX shares to every child in the US. He held about 6.42 billion shares in the company as of June.
“Next year, I will give one of my SpaceX shares to every kid in America. This will be the first of many,” Musk said in a post on X at the time.
“Giving shares, which are stakes in the future economy, directly to the people is the way,” said Musk, most of whose philanthropic efforts have been through the Musk Foundation, which reportedly holds more than $14bn in assets.
SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell and her husband in October pledged a share of their SpaceX stock to each of more than 2 million children under the Trump initiative.
