noticias.titulo: At odds over the EU budget, European leaders cut summit short
noticias.resumen: Even before they met, it was clear the gap between European leaders' demands for the EU budget would make negotiations difficult. They ended a summit meeting early and aim to agree on EU funding in December. DW has more.
noticias.texto:
At odds over budget, EU leaders break off summit early
Published November 26, 2026last updated November 27, 2026
What you need to know
- Special European Council meeting ends early after leaders disagree on budget
- Details of long-term budget, Ukraine's 2027 financial needs and ECB leadership were on the agenda
- Spaniard Pablo Hernandez de Cos to take over as head of the ECB
You can follow developments from the EU summit taking place on Thursday, November 26, below:
Antonia Costa wraps up EU summit that fails to close gaps in budget disputes
European Council President Antonio Costa said that 24 out of 27 members of the EU supported a proposal for a €45 billion loan for Ukraine.
That loan is split into two sections, with €20 billion to help finance for civil services and the other €25 billion going to arms and ammunition.
Euro News reported earlier in the day that Bulgaria reversed course and was ready to join the loan, so long as it was only paying into the part that wasn't covering Ukraine's military needs.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said there was considerable work to be done before a deal could be in place.
EU leaders cut short a second day of talks that was due to take place tomorrow and pushed discussions to another summit in December.
The disagreements over a shared EU budget for the years between 2028 and 2034 stem from different priorities among EU members.
Some countries prefer greater funding for defense and enhancing competitiveness, while others seek to keep in place funding for agriculture, among other issues.
EU leaders ultimately weren't able to reach an agreement at the end of Thursday.
Macron says Le Pen was 'arrogant' in speaking as if she was president already
French President Emmanuel Macron said far-right presidential candidate Marine Le Pen should be more humble after she criticized efforts to reach a deal on the EU budget before the end of the year.
EU leaders were gathered in Brussels throughout the day to see if they could hammer out an agreement over a shared budget from 2028 to 2034.
But they remain far apart on many issues, including some members opposing the use of funds for military aid to Ukraine.
During the day, Le Pen, who is projected to beat her centrist rivals in the April 2027 elections, accused Macron and the European Commission of trying to rush through a budget deal before next year.
"The apparent aim is to ‌deter us from defending France's interests in EU budget negotiations if the French people entrust us with the responsibility of governing," she said in a post on X.
Macron hit back, saying later: "Mrs. Le Pen is campaigning. It takes a peculiar kind of arrogance to think she’s already in charge of France's destiny. ‌Last I checked, she wasn’t elected."
Macron said he was careful to take into account the presidential election and that if there was no deal by December 31, negotiations would have to resume in the second half of 2027, when his successor would be in office.
"You have to be more humble when you're campaigning, even if you already see yourself in the job," Macron said.
No progress yet in EU budget talks, Dutch PM Rob Jetten says
EU leaders hadn't made as much progress in their discussions about the EU's next long-term budget, Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten said.
Jetten said it was up to EU Council President Antonio Costa to come up with an improvised proposal for the next budget, which he said would be debated in "more intense" negotiations in December.
EU leaders are still hoping to have another round of talks around midnight before calling it a day.
Like Germany, the Netherlands is a net contributor to the European Union.
EU budget talks delayed until December summit, Merz says
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said EU leaders will try to reach an agreement on the next multi-annual budget for the EU by the end of this year.
Merz said a day of talks among EU leaders in Brussels had brought "new movement" toward a reduction of the proposed size of the next budget, as demanded by Germany and other countries that are net contributors to the bloc's finances.
The leaders will try to hammer out a deal during a two-day summit starting December 17, Merz said.
Germany has been leading calls to attach a durable funding scheme for Ukraine to the EU's next budget.
Merz has made clear that his country would approve the next budget if all countries backed a loan for Ukraine.
Last year, the EU reached an agreement on a €90 billion loan to Ukraine through a compromise loan after a much-discussed frozen-asset plan failed.
The Czech Republic, Hungary and Slovakia opted out of backing the loan.
EU leaders to meet later tonight, Merz says
Contrary to earlier expectations, European Union leaders weren't quite done for the day, even if it was well past 2200 local time.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said that rather than meet again as scheduled on Friday, leaders would hold a final round of discussions around midnight and end the summit.
Thank you for following our coverage
Thank you for reading along with our coverage of the Euro Summit on Thursday.
We will be back tomorrow to bring you the latest from the second day.
Until then, you can watch DW's analysis of the event:
Hungary's Magyar sees 'virtually zero chance' of reaching a deal on Thursday
Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar has said the chances of reaching an agreement on Thursday are "virtually zero."
Leaders of the European Union are gathered today in Brussels to agree on the bloc's budget proposal for 2028 to 2034.
In an X post, Magyar said he outlined "Hungary’s priorities and the red lines" to the other member states.
"Having heard the completely opposing positions around the table, I would put the chances of reaching an agreement today at virtually zero," he wrote.
He also said "an agreement around Christmas looks unlikely" as well.
Pedro Sanchez welcomes nomination of Hernandez de Cos as new ECB chief
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez celebrated "a Spain that leads in Europe like never before," after the nomination of Pablo Hernandez de Cos as the next European Central Bank (ECB) chief.
Hernandez de Cos is set to become the new ECB head as the European Union (EU) leaders are gathered in Brussels for the Euro Summit.
Sanchez welcomed the news in a post on X, pointing out that the top EU positions held by Spanish officials Teresa Ribera, the European Commission's First Executive Vice-President, and Nadia Calvino, head of the European Investment Bank.
"In short, Spain leads in Europe like never before," he wrote.
Pablo Hernandez de Cos is set to become the new European Central Bank chief — reports
Spanish candidate Pablo Hernandez de Cos will become the next president of the European Central Bank (ECB), after being endorsed by the majority ‌of eurozone countries, news agencies reported.
As the leaders gather for the Euro Summit, the Financial Times first reported that de Cos will be the next ECB chief, citing people familiar with the matter. This was confirmed by Reuters and AFP, citing EU diplomat sources.
The decision came after the Netherlands said it would support the Spaniard as a consensus candidate.
Christine Lagarde has been president since November 2019 but has announced her intention to step down on February 7, 2027.
De Cos was up against Dutch central bank chief Klaas Knot for the presidency, while France's Laurence Boone and Germany's Markus Brunnermeier have been nominated for the ECB's two other top jobs.
Russia says EU budget plans would prolong war in Ukraine
Russia has criticized the European Union's proposed seven-year budget, accusing the bloc of seeking to prolong the war in Ukraine.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the EU's plans to allocate money for Ukraine in its budget would make Kyiv "less inclined toward a peace process and more determined to continue the war."
Peskov said the result would be more military spending, leaving less for governments to spend on school, hospitals and social facilities.
"This is not money for peace," Peskov said.
Support for Ukraine is among the key areas of discussion in the 2028-2034 budget which includes up to €100 billion for Ukraine, however diplomats say this figure falls well short of Kyiv's needs.
EU 'light-years' from budget deal, Italy PM Meloni says
Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has added her voice to those warning that European leaders have their work cut out for them when it comes to agreeing on a multi-year budget proposal.
"We're light-years ‌away from a ‌solution," Meloni told reporters ahead of the EU summit in Brussels.
"We are not willing to sign off on a budget under which ‌we would have to give more to receive less," she added.
Earlier, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the budget was "still too high" and that members states needed to be able to afford the full cost without taking on new debt.
Last week, European Council President Antonio Costa presented a new compromise proposal of €1.78 trillion ($1.95 trillion), around €204 billion lower than the initial proposal by the European Commission.
Analysis: The battle for Europe's future behind closed doors
Every seven years, European leaders gather in Brussels for what is arguably the most consequential negotiation cycle in the European Union. As German Chancellor Friedrich Merz put it upon arrival, it is about "the future of the European Union."
This is not a typical EU summit. The leaders of the 27 member states are confronting a question that will shape all angles of EU politics for years to come: How much money should the EU have, who should pay for it, and what should it be spent on?
It is the essence of EU summit diplomacy: a painstaking exercise in give-and-take, bargaining and compromise.
The European Commission laid down the opening bid over the summer. The proposal was ambitious. Brussels wants an EU budget that reflects a rapidly-changing world: more spending on defence, innovation, research, digital technologies and competitiveness. At the same time, that inevitably means pressure on some of the traditional pillars of EU spending, particularly agricultural subsidies and parts of the bloc's regional development programmes.
Since then, every member has arrived with a shopping list of demands.
Governments have pushed back against cuts, demanded new priorities, sought exemptions and fought for national interests. There have though also been others who are pushing FOR a reduction in spending, including Merz.
The original proposal from Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has already undergone numerous adjustments as negotiators attempted to accommodate competing demands.
The result is an extraordinarily complex puzzle.
At the centre of it all stands European Council President Antonio Costa. He will be shuttling between bilateral meetings with leaders, gather small groups behind closed doors and attempt to construct a package that gives everybody something they can take home and present as a victory.
For Costa, the stakes are high. Delivering an agreement would be a major test of his authority and reputation as the EU's chief broker. Especially as he was not made top negotiator for the EU in the peace talks on Russia's war in Ukraine. Diplomats expressed confidence in his fairness and negotiating skills before the summit, viewing him as someone capable of building trust among leaders who have differing priorities.
Yet nobody in Brussels expects an easy breakthrough. Many officials acknowledge that the pressure on member states may not yet be intense enough to force the final concessions required for a deal. Leaders are still defending red lines rather than crossing them.
So, this summit will highly likely end without a grand agreement. Leaders will probably decide to take stock of the latest negotiating proposals and return home to assess them in detail. There will be a new — and perhaps final — round on the next summit in December, a few days before Christmas.
WATCH: Is Gen Z really worse off than their parents?
As leaders grapple with long-term budgets, across Europe, young people are rising up. They're demanding better jobs, more funding for education and lower rents. The problems they are protesting are complex and often specific to their home country.
But there’s also a common message: Young people feel pessimistic about their economic future. A look at the data shows they could be right.
Bulgaria ready to back non-military aid for Ukraine
Bulgaria's Prime Minister Rumen Radev said his country would support a proposed €45 billion ($49 billion) EU loan to Ukraine, but only the funds earmarked for non-military aid.
"Bulgaria is going to take part in the loan of €20 billion (for) non-military support for Ukraine," Radev told reporters as he arrived at the EU summit in Brussels.
"We have a ‌huge historic diaspora of Bulgarians living in Ukraine, our wish is to concentrate our support in that area. We are going to contribute, but no money from Bulgaria for weapons," Radev said.
Last week European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the €45 billion would be split into two parts: ‌up to €25 billion for military aid and up to €20 billion for other ‌help as a means of getting member states to contribute where there were objections to funding weapons for Ukraine.
Germany's Merz says EU budget proposal 'still too high'
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said that the budget proposal for 2028 to 2034 was "still too too high" and did not provide the basis for an agreement, during comments made as he arrived at the summit.
"After all, the member states must be able to afford to pay for all of this," Merz said in Brussels.
The German leader also said the war in Ukraine needed to be ended as soon as possible and that the country needed help during a "very difficult winter."
Merz said that funding for Kyiv is "a task that we must also accomplish together,” and added: "The European Union consists of 27 member states, not 23 or 24."
Slovakia, the Czech Republic, and Hungary have been exempt from contributing to aid for Ukraine. The countries negotiated, as part of the current €90 billion loan for Ukraine, that they would not have financial obligations in guaranteeing the loan.
Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis did not agree with the German chancellor.
"Funding for Ukraine should be negotiated separately," said Babis, adding that his country needs the money for other expenditures. "I believe we will fight for this money," providing an early indication of how talks might proceed over the next two days.

noticias.titulo: Albania's youth are protesting in Flamingo Revolution, not leaving the country anymore
noticias.resumen: Youth protests against a rigid political system and corruption have shaken the government of Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama. They also show that fewer young people are willing to emigrate in search of a better future.
noticias.texto:
Albania's youth are protesting, not leaving the country anymore
November 26, 2026
In mid-October, students in the Albanian capital Tirana set a suitcase on fire and threw it into the courtyard of the Education Ministry. Everyone in the country understood the symbolism: According to the 2023 census, the population of this Western Balkan country shrunk by about 420,000 between 2011 and 2023 — by nearly 15% — primarily because of emigration.
For a generation of young Albanians, this was the response to a system that gave them little voice. But now young people want to stay, and the protesters are saying that the system has to change.
Known as the "Flamingo Revolution," the social movement began in May with demonstrations against a luxury resort in a coastal reserve that US President Donald Trump's daughter Ivanka Trump and her husband Jared Kushner were involved in.
It quickly evolved into broader criticism against corruption, Prime Minister Edi Rama's government and his ruling Socialist Party and the country's entire political class.
Thousands marched almost every evening for four months in protests that were largely peaceful. But on October 13, a student protest escalated and there were clashes with police. Since then, the unrest has continued, with police using tear gas, water cannons and rubber bullets against demonstrators. There have been hundreds of arrests and many injuries, amid damage to public and private property.
'Flamingo revolution' has broad support
The protesters have called for Rama's resignation, a transitional government, electoral reform and fresh elections. The movement, which has no leader, has support from people across the political spectrum. And while the prime minister has blamed "foreign hands" for the movement, there seems to be little evidence that external actors are orchestrating the protests, though they may have attempted to exploit the unrest online.
The protesters, who do not feel represented by Albania's democracy, are driven by domestic issues: corruption, the high cost of living and low wages. This is nothing new, but many factors have converged recently: a series of high-level corruption charges, including against ministers and two of Rama's former deputies, rising prices and the fact that Albania is being measured against EU standards by a new generation.
In certain areas, Rama has transformed Albania since taking office in 2013: the economy has grown significantly, as the government likes to point out, and tourism is booming. But the prosperity remains unevenly distributed. Critics accuse the government of channeling too much taxpayer money into a small number of well-connected companies through prestigious projects and public-private partnerships, and in some cases through corrupt business deals, at the expense of healthcare, education and better economic prospects for the wider population.
Rama has rejected the calls for his resignation and has invited protesters to engage in dialogue, which they have so far refused.
Alternating between Socialist and Democratic Party
In 2008, Rama and Sali Berisha, the long-time chairman of the opposition Democratic Party, worked on a reform to Albania's constitution and electoral law, which was approved by parliament. Since then, it is party leaders who have determined who enters Parliament, which weakens ties between lawmakers and their constituents.
In addition, it has become significantly more difficult for new parties to win seats. In 2025, a new party received about 64,000 votes, but only one seat. The Socialists, by contrast, won about one seat for every 10,000 votes.
Rama has been the leader of the Socialists since 2005, while Berisha first became the chairman of the Democratic Party in 1991. For 21 years, Albania's prime minister has either been Rama or Berisha. Freedom House, a US nongovernmental organization that promotes democracy worldwide, classifies Albania as "partly free" and describes the country's political parties as being "often organized around leading personalities."
Protesters on the streets have said that they want both men to be jailed. Rama has argued that governments should be replaced at the ballot box, not on the streets.
Though the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE) acknowledged that parliamentary elections in 2025 were "competitive and professionally managed" it said that they had taken place "in a highly polarized environment and contestants did not enjoy a level playing field."
It added that there were "reports of intimidation, misuse of public resources and pressure on public employees, which undermined equal opportunities."
The Democratic Party also spoke of election fraud and intimidation. Turnout was below 45%.
Protesters call out corruption, face high cost of living
Many protesters also allege that when it comes to business, what matters is the proximity to people in power. They criticize the public procurement, public auctions and concessions system, which has led to state-owned land, including coastal and protected areas, being sold to private investors.
Ordinary Albanians are feeling the financial brunt. According to the Albanian Institute of Statistics (INSTAT), half of all employees earn less than 60,000 lek (roughly €620 or $680) per month after taxes. But according to Eurostat, food prices are slightly above the EU average and real estate prices in Tirana have nearly doubled since 2018, with rents rising just as quickly.
For many years, young Albanians who were dissatisfied with the system opted to leave the country. The number of Albanian citizens in Germany more than doubled between 2018 and 2024, reaching almost 120,000.
Though it is still too early to say whether there are fewer Albanians leaving today, for many protesters staying has become a political statement.
Albanians largely pro-EU
Rama has argued that his resignation would jeopardize Albania's bid to join the European Union by 2030, but the vast majority of Albanians are pro-European, including those on the streets and in the opposition. From the protesters' perspective, it is the government headed by Rama that is the real obstacle on the path to the EU.
Though there is currently a wave of protests across Europe, the only obvious comparison is with Serbia, where a student-led movement recently forced a long-time ruler from office. Whether Albania will follow this example depends on whether young people, who have traditionally not been deeply engaged in politics, can turn their protests into votes.
What is certain is that for three decades, Albania's leaders have relied on their citizens' suitcases. Now, the country's students have burned that very luggage.
Andi Balla is a doctoral candidate at the Leibniz Institute for East and Southeast European Studies (IOS) in Regensburg, where he is conducting research on demographic debates in Albania. He has written numerous articles on Albania for an international audience.
This article was translated from German.

noticias.titulo: Gerard Depardieu to stand trial in France for rape and sexual assault
noticias.resumen: The Paris Court of Appeal upheld the order for the 77-year-old French actor to stand trial on charges of raping and sexually assaulting an actress in 2018.
noticias.texto:
Gerard Depardieu to stand trial in France for rape and sexual assault
November 26, 2026
French actor Gerard Depardieu failed in his attempt to overturn an order for him to stand trial on rape charges.
On Thursday, the Paris Court of Appeal ruled that Depardieu should face trial for the alleged rape and sexual assault that occurred on August 7, 2018. However, the court dismissed the allegations relating to a second incident that occurred six days later.
Depardieu still has the option of appealing to a higher court. His lawyer, Delphine Meillet, told the Associated Press that she disputes Thursday's ruling, though she did not specify whether she will challenge it in France's highest civil and criminal court.
This decision comes just two weeks after the 77-year-old Depardieu dropped his appeal against a sexual assault conviction in a separate case. He accepted an 18-month suspended prison sentence and issued a public apology.
What are the charges against Depardieu?
An actress, who was 22 years old at the time, accused Depardieu of raping and sexually assaulting her at his Paris apartment on August 7 and 13, 2018. Depardieu was 69 at the time of the alleged incident.
She reported the allegations to the police a few days later. Depardieu denies the allegations, claiming that the encounter was consensual.
Last year, a trial was ordered regarding the allegations. If the trial goes ahead, Depardieu could face up to 20 years in prison.
Carine Durrieu Diebolt, the victim's lawyer, said that the Thursday decision was a genuine relief and a victory for her client.
Accusations overshadow Depardieu's legacy
Depardieu was born in 1948 into a working-class family in Chateauroux, a city in central France. He overcame a speech impediment to become one of France's most prolific actors.
The film star was a dominant figure in French cinema for half a century, becoming a renowned cultural export. He earned an Oscar nomination for "Cyrano de Bergerac" and a Golden Globe for "Green Card."
Accusations of sexual misconduct and his subsequent conviction, however, have increasingly overshadowed his cinematic legacy.
The international media has also been paying attention to Depardieu's off-screen antics. One of the most notable instances was when he accepted a Russian passport from President Vladimir Putin in 2013 amid a dispute over French taxes.

noticias.titulo: Guinea-Bissau junta delays presidential vote for 2 years
noticias.resumen: The decision came exactly one year after the military took power on November 26, 2025. The junta said the conditions were insufficient to hold presidential elections for now.
noticias.texto:
Guinea-Bissau junta delays presidential vote for 2 years
November 26, 2026
The ruling junta in the West African nation of Guinea-Bissau announced Thursday that it is postponing elections by two years until November 26, 2028.
What do we know so far?
The decision came on the 1-year anniversary of the military takeover in Guinea-Bissau on November 26, 2025. The country is currently led by military general Horta Inta-a, who serves as transitional president.
Inta-a said in a statement that there was "an insufficiency of the technical, material and financial conditions" to hold the election.
"It is essential to guarantee effective conditions for preparing and holding elections in accordance with the principles of legality, democratic participation, equal opportunity, transparency and electoral integrity," he said.
The military coup in Guinea-Bissau came three days after a general election last year, with the military deposing incumbent President Umaro Sissoco Embalo. Both Embalo and opposition candidate Fernando Dias da Costa claimed victory in the election, with the military arresting Embalo one day prior to the results being released.
What's the political and human rights situation in Guinea-Bissau?
West African bloc ECOWAS has urged Guinea-Bissau to transition back to civilian rule.
Guinea-Bissau is a small tropical Portuguese-speaking nation on the West African coast which has seen multiple coups in its history. The country faces a high level of corruption and is also a key point for cocaine trafficking to Europe.
According to Washington DC-based think tank Freedom House, Guinea-Bissau is only "partly free" due to military interference in elections.
Reporters without Borders ranksGuinea-Bissau 100 out of 180 countries on its press freedom index, saying the "sharp deterioration of security for media professionals, combined with political and economic pressure, has severely tested the practice of journalism in recent years."

noticias.titulo: 'A lot of political theatre': EU summit ends in disarray as leaders cling to red lines
noticias.resumen: António Costa's attempt to prod EU leaders into ditching their red lines on the budget fell flat on Thursday as talks turned messy and bitter.
noticias.texto:
António Costa's attempt to prod EU leaders into ditching their red lines on the budget fell flat on Thursday as talks turned messy and bitter.
A summit specifically convened to find a breakthrough on the European Union's next budget ended in disarray after leaders, split in opposing camps, refused to abandon their red lines and openly questioned whether a deal could be reached by December.
The meeting was plagued by tensions, reproaches and even boycotts, raising serious questions on the leadership of European Council President António Costa, whose credibility now rests on whether these negotiations succeed or fail.
Costa's compromise proposalworth €1.78 trillion in current prices across seven years – a 10% cut from the original draft – was met with fierce pushback from all sides, taking the Council presidency aback.
"This meeting was a necessary step in the process. This is a negotiation process. It is normal that the different parties are starting to underline and mark their starting points. Everybody knows that we cannot fail Europe, and we need to have a new budget from the 1st of January 2028," Costa said at the press conference at the end of the summit.
The summit appeared doomed from the outset.
Leaders showed virtually no willingness to compromise as they made their way into Thursday's gathering and huddled with their respective groups.
On one side, the seven "Frugals", bent on slashing the budget. On the other side, the 17 "Friends of Cohesion", determined to push back against further cuts.
The tone was set by Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, who told reporters upon arrival that a deal on the seven-year budget was "light years away".
Meloni questioned Costa's much-repeated objective of reaching a deal by the end of the year to prevent the process from spilling over into the 2027 electoral cycle.
"I don't have a time limit. I have specific conditions," she said. "When the agreement is one that I consider valid and fair for Italy, then I'll sign it."
Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten, a staunch "frugal", was equally dismissive.
"There's no need to hurry," he said. "For me, there's no deadline."
The budget negotiations began around midday after leaders settled the matter of Christine Lagarde's succession as European Central Bank president. They first met all together in the main room, where they shared their well-known positions.
Nobody caved in during this session, waiting for others to move first, diplomats said.
Then, Costa split the summit into small groups of leaders. First, the "frugals", then the "cohesion friends", and then the six largest member states. After that, he began breakout sessions with geographically mixed leaders.
The proceedings increasingly frustrated the "frugals", who saw it as an attempt to pile pressure on them in favour of the "cohesion friends".
Feeling unfairly targeted, the "frugals" closed ranks and decided to boycott the small-group format, which Costa continued without their participation.
Meanwhile, French President Emmanuel Macron raised the stakes, calling a press conference to deliver a stark ultimatum: reach a deal by December or walk away empty-handed.
Macron warned that protracted negotiations risked becoming dangerously entangled in the French presidential campaign. Far-right firebrand Marine Le Pen, who is leading opinion polls, has vowed to slash France's contribution to the EU budget.
"I intend to make it very clear to our colleagues that, for political and democratic reasons, it will not be possible to reopen or conclude negotiations on the budget after 31st December," Macron said, decrying Costa's proposed cuts as a "strategic mistake".
"We are not prepared to reach a deal at any cost. We can conclude by 31st December, but that is the absolute limit."
Other member states consider Macron's threat of a future Le Pen presidency a tactic to extract concessions and eventually get his way, despite Costa's compromise widely seen as being overly French-friendly.
"That's quite rich," a diplomat quipped about the French reaction.
Macron's mid-summit appearance, a rare occurrence, wiped out chances of a breakthrough and precipitated the collapse of the talks.
In his own press conference, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz adopted a hardline "frugal" stance and vowed to slash the budget even further.
The deep political divide between Paris and Berlin, the EU’s two main powerhouses, has cast a shadow over the negotiations.
"Are we any further ahead? Yes and no. We are trying to define which direction it is going. I think I may say that," Merz told reporters.
The cuts to the budget, he said, will not stop at the €204 billion proposed by Costa. "It will become less," he added. "How much it will be then is open."
The fact that Costa announced early in the summit that the talks would not continue on Friday as originally planned dampened the energy among national delegations and immediately lowered expectations for a breakthrough, a diplomat said.
A second diplomat was more positive on the outcome of the summit, despite the messy proceedings. "You need to have a bad European Council to have a good one," they said. "It was a lot of political theatre. We did not have detailed negotiations."
Forgotten in the talks was Ukraine.
The summit was supposed to discuss a €45 billion support loan for the country, which faces a ballooning wartime deficit amid Russia's relentless attacks. But the budget fight sucked in all the energy and left Ukraine relegated to an afterthought.

noticias.titulo: Germany: Christmas markets open across the country amid tight security
noticias.resumen: Christmas markets across Germany are welcoming visitors with dazzling lights, traditional treats and festive attractions. Security remains a priority following deadly attacks in recent years.
noticias.texto:
Germany's Christmas markets are drawing crowds as the country's roughly 3,000 festive venues prepare for an estimated 170 million visits this season. In Berlin, skaters glide beneath the television tower beside a brightly lit Ferris wheel, while Munich and Cologne welcome visitors against some of Germany's most recognisable architectural backdrops.
Munich's Christkindlmarkt, a tradition dating back to the 14th century, features 138 stalls selling gingerbread, wooden carvings and festive decorations. A dedicated nativity market and the traditional Krampus run complement the celebrations, which continue until Christmas Eve.
At the foot of Cologne Cathedral, more than 140 red-roofed stalls surround a 25-metre fir tree decorated with some 50,000 lights. The market offers traditional crafts, mulled wine and more than 100 free performances until 23 December.
Despite heightened security following the deadly attacks in Berlin in 2016 and Magdeburg in 2024, the German capital continues to embrace its festive traditions. Berlin alone hosts more than 80 Christmas markets, ranging from torchlit medieval fairs with fire shows to Alt-Rixdorf’s charity market, which opens for just one weekend each December.

noticias.titulo: Thanksgiving storms flood US coasts and disrupt holiday travel
noticias.resumen: Macy's has postponed its 100th parade in Manhattan as more than 600,000 homes and businesses lost power.
noticias.texto:
Macy's has postponed its 100th parade in Manhattan as more than 600,000 homes and businesses lost power.
Storms brought flooding and strong winds to parts of the United States on Thanksgiving, complicating holiday travel.
Streets were inundated in New Jersey's Sea Isle City and Ocean City, while water spread across parts of Avalon. Borough of Avalon business administrator Scott J. Wahl said the town was seeing some of the worst flooding in its history. A few drivers had to be rescued after driving around barricades and into floodwaters, but no injuries were reported, Wahl said.
At Philadelphia International Airport, aircraft were seen stranded on the tarmac amid the bad weather. The National Weather Service warned of disruption at eastern US airports through Friday morning, citing poor visibility, turbulence, strong winds and ice forming on aircraft.
Wind gusts of 80 km/h or higher were expected along the Interstate 95 corridor. All of New Jersey was under a state of emergency declared by Governor Mikie Sherrill, and parts of New York were under one declared by Governor Kathy Hochul. More than 600,000 homes and businesses were without electricity on Thursday afternoon, mostly in East Coast states, according to the outage tracking website poweroutage.us.
Macy's postponed its 100th Thanksgiving Day Parade in Manhattan until Saturday. It said it acted in an abundance of caution after consulting city officials, amid worries about how the parade's giant balloons would fare in the wind.
Rain and snow also affected the St. Louis area in Missouri, where up to 33 cm of snow was expected. In Wentzville, Missouri, heavy snow partly collapsed the roof of the Wentzville Ice Arena.
On the West Coast, coastal flood warnings were issued from Southern California to the Oregon and Washington coasts because of king tides. These occur when the gravitational pulls of the moon and sun align to raise water levels. A wave tore down part of a pier in Pacifica, California, on Wednesday.
Although both coasts of the US were affected, travel is usually busier in the days leading up to Thanksgiving than on the holiday itself.

noticias.titulo: France's presidential hopefuls speak to Euronews as they court local politicians for endorsements
noticias.resumen: Although around forty figures have so far declared their intent to run in the presidential election — or are seen as potential candidates — not all will go the full way.
noticias.texto:
Although around forty figures have so far declared their intent to run in the presidential election — or are seen as potential candidates — not all will go the full way.
Five months ahead of France’s presidential elections, the country’s annual mayoral congress transformed into a political hunting ground as candidates sought to win over local officials and get their endorsements this week.
Although around forty figures have so far declared their intent to run in the presidential election — or are seen as potential candidates — not all will go the full way. To qualify, they must secure at least 500 endorsements from elected officials, with mayors representing the largest pool of potential sponsors.
After nearly a decade of Emmanuel Macron's presidency, France's government has been criticised for concentrating power and decision-making at the national level. Against this backdrop, candidates have been seeking to demonstrate their local roots and build support among rural communities.
David Lisnard: 'rules are like cholesterol'
David Lisnard, the mayor of Cannes, was re-elected on Wednesday as head of the Association of Mayors of France (AMF), while pursuing his presidential ambitions with his conservative Nouvelle Énergie party.
Speaking to Euronews, he warned that democracy was under attack from both external and internal threats, calling for a stronger role for local government and praising grassroots politics.
France's mayoral association brings together the mayors of some 34,000 French municipalities, most of whom are elected without a partisan party label.
"We must regain the ability to act and let the local level show the way," said Lisnard, while criticising excessive bureaucracy, red tape and contradictory regulations.
He added that "rules and standards are necessary, but like cholesterol or technocrats, too much is harmful."
Meanwhile, on foreign policy, he warned against "illiberal empires" with expansionist ambitions, naming Russia and China, while also calling out radical Islamism.
A fragmented political race
Lisnard's standing in the polls has risen in recent weeks, amid divisions within the centre-right bloc.
Certain polling scenarios have placed him ahead of former Prime Minister Édouard Philippe, who was previously viewed as a potential challenger to the far-right National Rally party's Marine Le Pen in a second round.
Polls indicate that Le Pen is currently heading the presidential race, followed by the left's Jean-Luc Mélenchon with his France Unbowed party on the left.
Lisnard is campaigning on a programme centred on cutting public spending and taxes, easing business regulations and sharply reducing immigration — leading Le Pen to accuse him of seeking to "grind down" workers' rights with his labour and social policies.
He has also cited Argentine President Javier Milei as an example of radical economic reform and pledged to “turn off the tap” on immigration.
Lisnard has also faced criticism over allegations that he is using his position at the head of the AMF, which he has led since 2021, to advance his presidential ambitions and secure the endorsements needed to qualify for the race.
'All eyes in Europe are on our country'
Former French Prime Minister Dominique de Villepin, who failed to secure the 500 endorsements required to stand in the 2012 presidential election, has called for a "strong France", which can restore its credibility.
He told Euronews that it was vital for France to address its "triple" debt,calling for a strong country that "regains its credibility and regains its health".
"We have a significant financial debt to settle", he stressed, while also pointing to an ecological debt and social debt in "a country where inequalities are increasing".
Meanwhile, centre-left presidential hopeful Raphaël Glucksmann, leader of the Place Publique party, told Euronews that "the eyes of Europe are on France" ahead of its elections.
Referring to the 18 November summit involving Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, he described the three leaders as "masters of the world who intend to share it."
He argued that "the only obstacle" to this division of the world was "a powerful, independent and free Europe". France, he said, would be "the cornerstone of this Europe", adding that this was "the most important issue at stake in the election."

noticias.titulo: UK: London's Gingerbread City returns with 50 edible architectural creations
noticias.resumen: London architects have created a miniature city featuring gingerbread skyscrapers, sugar rivers and iconic landmarks. The festive exhibition also explores the future of urban living.
noticias.texto:
Unveiled on 26 November 2026, the tenth edition of The Gingerbread City brings together 50 architectural creations, from intricately crafted replicas of famous landmarks to futuristic skyscrapers. Among the highlights is a miniature Royal Albert Hall, painstakingly recreated by architect Zak Wharton using computer-aided design to capture the building's distinctive symmetry. Gingerbread bridges cross rivers of blue sugar, marshmallow monsters roam snowy landscapes and Father Christmas stretches between towering buildings.
Organised by the Museum of Architecture, this year's exhibition takes "Future Forward" as its theme, challenging architects to imagine how buildings might adapt to climate change and improve people's wellbeing. A futuristic skyscraper named SpireHive explores innovations such as living algae and self-healing concrete. The exhibition also features a partnership with homelessness charity St Mungo's, for which former Great British Bake Off contestant Carol Pui Man Li has created five structures inspired by the experiences of people who have faced homelessness. Celebrating its tenth anniversary, The Gingerbread City opens to the public at Space House in Holborn on 28 November and runs until 3 January 2027.

noticias.titulo: Belgium: Farmers and tractors descend on Brussels to defend EU subsidies
noticias.resumen: Around 200 representatives of European farming unions marched through Brussels, Belgium, on Thursday 26 November 2026 to protest against proposed cuts to the European Union's Common Agricultural Policy (CAP). The demonstration coincided with a summit on the bloc's next long-term budget.
noticias.texto:
Rolling into Brussels’ European quarter alongside a convoy of tractors, protesters marched past the European Parliament with banners demanding that agricultural funding be protected, one machine bearing a stark placard reading "Agriculture for sale, €0". Chanting slogans against looming cuts, demonstrators echoed warnings from farming unions that subsidies could drop by 20% under the EU’s next long-term budget, tightening the squeeze on already strained rural incomes — a plight underscored by Lucas Bierlaire of the Walloon Farmers Federation, who warned that many growers were already struggling to make a decent living.
The rally coincided with a two-day summit in which EU leaders are locked in fractious talks over the bloc’s 2028-2034 budget, divided over the European Commission’s proposed €2 trillion spending plan that would substantially erode agricultural support in real terms. Arnaud Rousseau, head of France’s largest farming union, the FNSEA, urged Brussels to show greater ambition for European agriculture despite fiscal pressures, ahead of a follow-up summit in mid-December aimed at sealing a deal before the year’s end.

noticias.titulo: UK-EU food deal carries exit penalty, legal text shows
noticias.resumen: Political parties Reform UK and the Conservatives have both signalled they would consider unpicking Andy Burnham's Brexit reset if they win power at the next general election in 2029.
noticias.texto:
Political parties Reform UK and the Conservatives have both signalled they would consider unpicking Andy Burnham's Brexit reset if they win power at the next general election in 2029.
Britain and the European Union would each have to pay to rebuild border checks if they walked away from their new food and drink deal within the first 10 years, according to the legal text published on Thursday.
The termination clause requires whichever side quits early to cover "reasonable and proportionate costs" of restoring the infrastructure the deal removes. Any dispute over the bill would go to an international tribunal, UK officials said.
"That termination clause is a standard practice in international treaties, and this one applies equally to both sides, including the EU," Prime Minister Andy Burnham's deputy spokesperson told reporters.
The sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) agreement was one of three deals Burnham signed with EU leaders in Brussels, Belgium, on 20 November. The other two link the two sides' carbon markets and allow young people to study and work across borders.
The government says the SPS deal, due to take effect in 2028, could add £5.1 billion to the UK economy by cutting red tape on food and drink exports.
The clause was published days after Reform UK leader Nigel Farage vowed to "repeal" the reset. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said on Thursday she "does not support" it.
Charles Grant, director of the Centre for European Reform think tank, told AFP the provision was "an insurance policy" for the EU, given Britain's continuing debate over its relationship with the bloc.
Legislation to put the deals into effect was introduced in parliament on Thursday, and MPs are due to debate it on 7 December. It would align the UK with EU rules in the sectors covered. British experts would be consulted on new laws but would have no vote, which critics say makes Britain a "rule taker".
Burnham, who replaced Keir Starmer in July, has said the agreements are probably the most that can be achieved in this parliament. He plans a year of informal brainstorming with EU leaders before setting out options for the long-term relationship. These range from keeping things as they are to rejoining the bloc, which he has said would be "unthinkable" without a referendum.

noticias.titulo: Son of Myanmar's Suu Kyi 'relieved' by first call in five years, questions military's motives
noticias.resumen: Speaking to Euronews’ The World Conversation, Kim Aris described his relief at hearing his mother’s voice after five years, called for tougher sanctions enforcement and defended her record on the Rohingya genocide ruling.
noticias.texto:
Speaking to Euronews’ The World Conversation, Kim Aris described his relief at hearing his mother’s voice after five years, called for tougher sanctions enforcement and defended her record on the Rohingya genocide ruling.
Aung San Suu Kyi's son says he was relieved to hear his mother's voice for the first time in five years but remains concerned about her condition after Myanmar's military moved the 81-year-old to house arrest at an undisclosed location, questioning whether the gesture was genuine.
Kim Aris, who has campaigned for his mother's release since the military seized power in 2021, speaking at universities and meeting with governments to press for action, spoke to Euronews' The World Conversation after the call — the first contact the family had had with her in five years.
"Obviously I was very happy to hear her voice and it was a huge relief to actually know that she's alive and well after all this time," Aris said, adding that for two or three years the family had not even known whether she was alive.
Aris, who holds British citizenship through his late father, academic Michael Aris, said he had run a proof-of-life campaign last year, and that the Red Cross visited her earlier this year and confirmed she was alive.
The call was arranged after the Myanmar embassy in London contacted the British Foreign Office the week before it took place, Aris said. It was recorded and monitored, and the two kept to family matters. His mother's first question was whether he had been looking after himself.
"They call this house arrest, but I do not call this a house arrest. She's not in her own home. She's allowed no access to any sort of media, as far as I'm aware," Aris said.
He said she had been held in solitary confinement in a prison in the capital Naypyidaw, with access only to military doctors and no contact with anyone outside military or police personnel.
He said the military was using the transfer to project an image of moderation and urged the international community to maintain pressure rather than re-engage.
"The military have been able to circumnavigate these sanctions for all of this time, and they're still receiving the money and the weaponry that they need to suppress their people," he told Euronews.
No return to civilian rule yet, Aris says
Suu Kyi led the National League for Democracy to a landslide election victory in 2020 and served as Myanmar's de facto head of government. The military refused to recognise the result, seized power in February 2021 and has held her ever since.
The coup triggered a civil war in which pro-democracy forces and ethnic armed groups have taken control of large parts of the country.
More than 4 million people are internally displaced and a further 2 million have fled abroad, Aris said, in part due to conscription laws introduced by the military.
Min Aung Hlaing, who led the coup, was elected president in April by the military-dominated parliament. Aris dismissed suggestions that the country was returning to civilian rule.
"The so-called elections that they held at the end of last year or the beginning of this year were so far from being free and fair," he said.
Asked why young people had taken up arms despite Suu Kyi's commitment to non-violence, Aris said the military had left them no alternative.
"When they came out in peaceful protests at the start of the coup, they were shot in the streets," he said.
He called on the military to stop bombing civilians and release all political prisoners as conditions for peace. "Without those steps, I can't see peace coming back to Burma soon," he said.
'Trying to hold together a very fragile democracy'
Last Thursday, the International Court of Justice ruled for the first time that Myanmar had committed genocide against its Rohingya Muslim minority during a military crackdown in 2017.
The court ordered Myanmar to pay reparations, ensure the safe return of displaced Rohingya and prosecute those responsible.
On Monday, the UK formally recognised the genocide, sanctioned five senior Myanmar military officers and announced plans to restrict aviation fuel supplies to the country.
Min Aung Hlaing has since said his government would reject some of the court's demands, describing the case as a "one-sided accusation".
Suu Kyi appeared before the ICJ in December 2019 to defend Myanmar against the genocide allegations.
Aris defended the decision, saying his mother established the Kofi Annan Commission on the Rakhine State on the second day of her term in office, before the issue drew wider international attention.
"They say that she went to The Hague to defend the military. That's just not the case," he said. "She was trying to hold together a very fragile democracy, which the military could have dismantled at any point, which they have done now."
Five years after the coup, Aris said he believed his mother could still play a role in rebuilding Myanmar.
"It's very hard to know what the situation in Burma will be like in 10 years. I hope that the civil war will have finished and democracy will have been re-established," Aris said.
"And whilst I know my mother will always be involved one way or another, I hope she's able to take a step back and look after herself a bit more."

noticias.titulo: Argentina enters technical recession as weak consumption undermines Milei's economic gains
noticias.resumen: Argentina's economy shrank 1.8% in the third quarter, its second straight contraction. Weak consumption, falling purchasing power and strain in key sectors are slowing growth and clouding Javier Milei's prospects.
noticias.texto:
Argentina's economy shrank 1.8% in the third quarter, its second straight contraction. Weak consumption, falling purchasing power and strain in key sectors are slowing growth and clouding Javier Milei's prospects.
Argentina's economy has entered a technical recession after two consecutive quarters of contraction, despite the solid performance of key sectors such as oil and mining. The Monthly Economic Activity Indicator (EMAE), published by the National Institute of Statistics and Census (Indec), shows a fall of 1.8% between July and September, after the 1% decline recorded in the second quarter.
Although activity picked up by 1.1% in September compared with the previous month, it was still 1.2% below the level of the same month in 2025. The final gross domestic product (GDP) figures, which will make it possible to confirm officially how the economy is evolving, will be published on 16 December.
The government of Javier Milei has called for caution before declaring that the country is in recession. However, economists believe that the EMAE data clearly point to that situation, as they show two consecutive quarters of contraction.
Weak domestic demand
The downturn is largely due to weak domestic demand, which contrasts with the growth of activities linked to the exploitation of natural resources. In September, the hydrocarbons and mining sectors grew by 11.1% year on year, but their momentum was not enough to offset the declines in other branches of activity.
Among the most affected sectors is fishing, with a collapse of 48.6%. Agriculture also fell, by 2%, and manufacturing industry by 1.8%. These activities carry considerable weight in Argentina's economy, so their poor results offset the dynamism of energy and mining exports.
The fall in consumption is another of the main factors behind the contraction. Buying on instalments, which had sustained part of demand in recent years, has lost steam. At the same time, interest rates on personal loans are around 64% a year and around six million people have fallen into arrears.
Loss of purchasing power and a labour market under strain
Price trends also make it harder to restore purchasing power. Although inflation has fallen considerably from the 211% year-on-year rate recorded in 2023, forecasts for 2026 have worsened. At present, an average price rise of 31% is expected, compared with the 22.4% that was anticipated at the start of the year. In October, monthly inflation stood at 2.2%, up from 1.9% in September.
Wages have seen only a limited recovery. According to consultancy LCG, registered pay improved by 2.5% in real terms up to September, compared with December last year. However, it remains below November 2023 levels, especially in the public sector, where it has fallen by 15.4%.
The economic deterioration is also reflected in the labour market. Unemployment reached 7.9% in the second quarter of 2026, its highest level since Milei arrived at the Casa Rosada. In addition, the economy shed more than 300,000 jobs in the private sector and nearly 70,000 in the public sector, while around 30,000 companies closed, according to official figures.
Milei's economic challenges for 2027
The recession represents a setback for the Argentine president's economic programme, although it does not wipe out some of his main results, such as the first fiscal surplus in 14 years, achieved in 2024, and the sharp reduction in inflation.
On top of domestic difficulties comes a deterioration in market confidence. Argentina's country risk recently exceeded 1,100 points, its highest level since 2025, while the official dollar rate passed 1,630 pesos.
Growth prospects have also weakened. According to the newspaper 'El Tiempo' the consultancy LCG expects GDP to grow by at most 0.7% in 2026, far from the 3% target set by the government. For 2027, while the executive projects growth of 4%, its estimates put the increase at around 1.5%.
The combination of weak consumption, lagging wages and difficulties in key sectors therefore poses one of the main challenges for Milei's economic policy and his re-election ambitions.

noticias.titulo: Budget summit walkout leaves EU one month to salvage deal
noticias.resumen: No one expected an agreement at Thursday's gathering — but the scale of division caused leaders to depart visibly shocked and angry.
noticias.texto: BRUSSELS — A summit of EU leaders descended into crisis after governments demanding a smaller seven-year budget snubbed European Council President António Costa by walking out of his negotiation sessions. The dramatic late-night move at Thursday’s gathering in Brussels heaps pressure on Costa, who was tasked with brokering a deal between the EU’s 27 governments and who is desperate to reach a positive outcome before the end of the year. While EU officials with knowledge of the process were caught off guard by the severity of the division, many had predicted some kind of political theater and still didn’t rule out a compromise emerging when leaders meet again on Dec. 17. “All that effort, all the political fanfare, all the big announcements — and absolutely nothing to show for it,” Bernd Lange, chair of the European Parliament’s trade committee, said in a post on X . Costa hadn’t organized Thursday’s summit to get a deal. Rather, his goal was to bang heads together and try to bridge splits between the two main rival camps: those like Spain and Italy, that want a bigger budget and to protect “traditional” EU spending in areas such as farming and poorer regions, and those like Germany and Sweden demanding the bloc scales down its ambitions and refocuses investment toward defense and security. But after hours of meetings among small groups of leaders, several countries pushing for budget cuts — Denmark, Sweden, Belgium and Austria — walked out, claiming this negotiating method was aimed at pitching them against each other. “It was obvious this was a move to divide us, to buy each of us seven off with a gift,” a diplomat from a country that wants a smaller budget said. “It just went really badly. It was not a real discussion.” They were granted anonymity, like others in this article, to speak candidly about the dramatic unfolding. Costa abandoned plans to return for a second day and cut his concluding 1 a.m. press conference with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen to just 11 minutes. ‘Strategic mistake’ The EU’s 27 leaders will now make a push to secure a deal at December’s summit, which multiple diplomats and officials said will probably last several days and nights. While technically the bloc has an entire year to reach agreement on what’s called the Multiannual Financial Framework for 2028-2034, the current leadership are determined to get it settled before April’s election in France, where the far-right leader Marine Le Pen is the favorite to become president. A visibly angry Emmanuel Macron criticized Costa’s proposed cuts as “a strategic mistake”for Europe ― a signal that threading the needle between the two camps won’t be easy. Macron warned that dragging negotiations into the new year “is not democratically possible” as it would be too close to the election. Underscoring that direction of travel, Costa indicated in the closed-door meetings with leaders that he will put forward a new budget proposal — envisaging fresh cuts — over the coming weeks to try to bring the EU closer to a deal, said two EU diplomats. ‘Mr. Blackmail’ But in a further sign the choreography was getting derailed, other leaders started to distance themselves from the year-end deadline. “I don’t have a deadline, I have conditions,” said Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, who frequently disagrees with Macron but who’s on the side of a larger budget. “When there is an agreement that I consider fair for Italy, I will sign it. Until then, I am not prepared to sign anything.” In another rebuke of Macron’s ultimatum, one EU diplomat nicknamed the French president “Monsieur Chantage” (Mr. Blackmail). “It’s rich to come here and take hostage the negotiations because of your national election,” the diplomat said. The Commission initially proposed a budget of around €2 trillion. Ahead of this week’s summit, Costa proposed to slash it by €204 billion. But that won’t be the end of it. Costa told leaders that he’s planning to cut the Commission’s proposal by between another €220 billion to €230 billion — which is not far from the demands of the “frugal” countries, the diplomat said. He indicated that reductions will overwhelmingly affect competitiveness and foreign aid, as opposed to regional spending and agriculture. “We’re not hugely far apart, but those last-minute solutions will matter a lot,” Petteri Orpo, prime minister of Finland — a country in the smaller budget camp — told reporters. He proposed €250 billion cuts from the Commission’s plan. ‘Really angry’ Costa’s tactics at the summit seemed to have disappointed both sides. His strategy of bringing together small groups of leaders “was not the best idea” because governments felt reluctant to reveal their red lines in front of their rivals, a diplomat from a country pushing for a larger budget said. The decision to boycott the later meetings came after Finland’s Orpo grew “really angry” with Costa’s approach during one session, one EU diplomat said. “Members of the S7 [the self-declared “Sensible Seven” of governments wanting a smaller budget] attended two breakout sessions, after which we concluded that further sessions would not bring us closer to a solution,” Austria wrote in a statement. After the summit, Costa played down the apparent fiasco and said that the 10-hour discussion with leaders “was very useful to figure out the parameters of a possible landing zone in December.” By the time Costa confirmed to reporters in the early hours of Friday that leaders “didn’t reach an agreement” most had already left for the night. “We will continue to work,” he said. Sebastian Starcevic, Aude van den Hove, Kathryn Carlson, Bjarke Smith-Meyer, Marianne Gros, Martina Sapio, Gerardo Fortuna, Jacopo Barigazzi, Hans von der Burchard, Tim Ross, Agnes Rønberg, Max Griera, Bartosz Brzeziński, Thibault Krause and Camille Gijs contributed reporting.

noticias.titulo: Macron accuses ‘arrogant’ Le Pen of speaking as if she already won
noticias.resumen: Le Pen feels she's being cut out of EU budget negotiations. Macron reminded her that he's still in charge.
noticias.texto: BRUSSELS — French President Emmanuel Macron thinks Marine Le Pen should learn to know her place. Macron on Thursday rejected criticism from the far-right presidential candidate, who is accusing him and EU institutions of deliberately rushing negotiations over the bloc’s 2028-2034 budget to make sure she doesn’t have a say in them. “Ms. Le Pen is campaigning just like other candidates. It is a strange kind of arrogance to think that she is already in charge of France’s destiny because, until proven otherwise, she has not been elected, and yours truly is elected until May 13, 2027. ” Macron told reporters. Macron urged more “humility” from Le Pen, stressing that she is not in office yet. While he hopes that EU leaders can reach a budget deal soon, the French president has warned that , if negotiations are not wrapped up by the end of the year, he will stop participating and leave that task to his successor — which may be Le Pen. “After December 31, I will not be in a position — from a political or democratic standpoint—to reopen a discussion on the budget and bring it to a conclusion. We will be entering a period that is far too close to the presidential election in France,” he said on Thursday. Macron already had the same reaction when, in 2024, Le Pen claimed that Macron should refrain from picking the next French EU commissioner during a parliamentary election campaign. On Thursday evening, the French President appeared extremely disappointed by the direction negotiations were taking and by cuts proposed by the European Council President António Costa and pushed by frugal countries. “Europe is making a strategic mistake,” he warned.

noticias.titulo: Trump diverges from NATO statement, emphasizing Ukraine mustn’t expand war
noticias.resumen: The U.S. president's unilateral tweak of a joint missive occurred days after Kyiv struck a Russian warship off the coast of Libya.
noticias.texto: BRUSSELS — Donald Trump sprung a surprise on NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte after the two met in Florida amid the U.S. president’s latest push to end the war between Ukraine and Russia. Following the Wednesday night meeting at Mar-a-Lago, the two leaders said they had “discussed the importance of Russia avoiding any actions that intentionally, or unintentionally, expand the war, and the importance of obtaining a peaceful resolution to the war as rapidly as possible” in a joint statement shared by both the White House and NATO . Writing hours later on Truth Social , the president altered the tone of the remark by adding two words — changing the statement to say “Russia and Ukraine” must avoid such actions. A NATO official, who was granted anonymity to speak freely about the sensitive issue, said the original missive was the officially agreed statement between the two sides — signaling Trump had later amended the statement unilaterally. The White House didn’t respond to a request for comment from POLITICO. The addition is pointed, coming days after Ukraine struck a Russian warship in a Libyan port, thousands of kilometers from Kyiv. The attack, which legal experts say may have broken international law , has drawn no criticism from most of Ukraine’s allies given Russia’s daily bombardment against its neighbor. It also highlights persistent tensions between Trump and Volodymyr Zelenskyy, the Ukrainian leader who has refused to abandon Kyiv’s long-range strikes against Russian refineries and critical infrastructure. Trump last month said it was “time for Ukraine to get a new President” — blaming Zelenskyy for holding up a peace deal. That posture marks a contrast to Trump’s recent overtures toward Russian President Vladimir Putin, whom he referred to as a “friend” during last week’s trilateral meeting with the Kremlin boss and Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Shenzhen. Russian strikes have, for years, continuously targeted Ukrainian energy infrastructure. The updated language also throws up a fresh challenge for Rutte. The former Dutch prime minister has repeatedly lavished praise on the American president in public as he scrambles to maintain U.S. arms shipments and limited support for Ukraine, and unity inside NATO. But the divergence showcases how his approach to keep Trump on message has clear limits. Despite the Truth Social addition pointing to Ukraine, Trump later added he had “spent a lot of time talking about the fact that I would like to see President Putin pull back all Military aggression against territories throughout Europe” during the meeting. Attention will now turn to a NATO foreign ministers meeting in Brussels on Dec. 2, which allies had previously expected to line up with a long-anticipated U.S. review of its troop presence in Europe. The U.S. has since told allies the revamp would be delayed . The Trump-Rutte meeting was originally intended to center around the overhaul, dubbed the Europe Posture Review, the NATO official said, but instead focused on transatlantic defense industrial scale-up and Russian hybrid attacks in Europe as the review’s publication was postponed. Joe Stanley-Smith contributed to this report.

noticias.titulo: EU leaders leave Brussels with no budget deal, piling pressure on Christmas summit
noticias.resumen: The so-called 'frugal' EU states want deeper cuts, the 'Friends of Cohesion' group wants agriculture and regional funding spared, and Antonio Costa's €204bn compromise satisfies no one.
noticias.texto: EU leaders failed to reach agreement on the bloc’s next long-term budget at a summit on Thursday night (26 November) in Brussels, where the so-called frugal countries and pro-cohesion camp remained far apart. Negotiations were based on a new, substantially-reduced, budget compromise that is 10.3 percent, or €204bn in current prices, below the nearly €2 trillion EU Commission proposal for 2028-34. But a group of net payer countries, led by Germany, wanted further cuts to the budget. “It will not remain at €204bn. It will be less,” German chancellor Friedrich Merz told reporters late at night. “I have always made my position clear. The reduction compared to the commission proposal must be several hundred billion euros.” And Merz then made clear that “in nominal terms, €200bn is at the very bottom end of what can be considered ‘several’,’’ – suggesting he’d like to see substantial further reductions to the size of the budget. His French counterpart Emmanuel Macron however described the €204 billion reduction as a “strategic error”. “We are effectively setting ourselves up for a decline in European public investment compared to China, and France does not support any additional cuts,” he said as he left the summit early. Despite his wish for a larger EU budget, Macron also made clear France would not contribute more to the EU budget. “We all hope to stabilise national contributions. That’s the challenge we have before us,” he said. And the French president also rejected Dutch suggestions of reducing the EU’s agriculture fund to free up cash for innovation and competitiveness, saying that France instead wants to postpone repaying Covid-era debt to “give more ambition to the budget, and reduce national contributions”. Read more A ‘bad’ summit first, an EU budget deal later Measuring size Not all were unhappy about the size of EU Council president Antonio Costa’s budget proposal, however. Cypriot president Nikos Christodoulides, for his part, called the overall 10-percent cut “a very logical compromise.” Measured against the EU’s economic output, Costa’s budget proposal comes in at 1.07 percent of gross national income (GNI), below the 1.12 percent of the current budget agreed in 2020. If Covid-era repayments are subtracted, the budget is even smaller comparatively, at around 0.97 percent of GNI. That would make the next budget substantially smaller than the current one, which expires at the end of 2027. But net contributing countries, a group that also includes the Netherlands, Austria, Sweden, Denmark and Finland, with Belgium as an ‘associate member’ want nominal size to shrink, and have called on Costa to present another budget with further cuts. “He [Costa] really has to, because we cannot afford this,” a senior diplomat of one of the frugal countries said. The biggest disagreement however wasn’t about size of the budget, but about where the axe should fall. Everybody knew what not to cut Phrased differently, everybody had a strong opinion about what not to cut, but almost nobody knew what should or could be cut. A large group of 17 ‘Friends of Cohesion’, mostly central, eastern and southern net recipients (those who get more from the budget than they pay in), resisted cuts to agriculture and cohesion. Czech prime minister Andrej Babiš, one of them, vowed to “fight” for cohesion funds. Austrian chancellor Christian Stocker, a member of the frugal squad, also insisted on a smaller budget, but rejected any suggestion to reduce the size of the agriculture budget. In a move seen as a negotiation tactic, Germany’s Merz didn’t specifically take aim at any of the envelopes. The Dutch were the exception and knew exactly where the cuts should be made: in the “old-fashioned policies” of cohesion and agriculture. noticias.titulo: A ‘bad’ summit first, an EU budget deal later
noticias.resumen: Everyone at the summit insists their red lines are unbreakable — yet the real story is how far they will bend once the ticking clock, Ukraine’s bills and looming 2027 elections start to crush their resolve.
noticias.texto: Budget talks in Brussels are expected to run late on Thursday (26 November) as EU leaders clash over how big the next seven-year budget should be, who foots the bill and whether all 27 must pay for Ukraine – with time running short to reach a deal before the end of the year. On the table is a nearly €2 trillion budget for 2028-2034. But no deal was really ever expected to come out of this special European Council. In line with an unspoken Brussels tradition, EU Council president António Costa knew he needed a ‘bad’ summit before a ‘good’ one would even be possible. At the last EU budget negotiations, the ‘special summit’ in February 2020 failed – without even clarifying next steps. The real deal only came after a five-day summit five months later in July 2020 – a pattern that could be repeated this December if a deal is achieved then, as Costa hopes (having previously warned that he could stay until Christmas to make the deal happen). Costa’s cuts reduce the overall size of the next budget for 2028-2034 by €204bn, compared with the European Commission’s initial proposal. Notably, new priorities that need financing, such as research or innovation, have received the biggest cuts, alongside development aid, because agriculture and regional funds are politically too important for a majority of EU leaders. Read more Less EU money for farmers and regions, but a growing Ukraine bill: Leaders meet to square trillion-euro circles at special summit EU budgets always come in at a little above one percent of gross national income (GNI), as so-called ‘frugal’ countries (some of those who pay more to the budget than they receive) refuse to go higher. Costa’s proposal is close at 0.97 percent of GNI, with pandemic recovery debt repayments subtracted. ‘Cheap’ is an expensive mistake But many feel the budget is too small. “Europe is making a strategic mistake,” French president Emmanuel Macron said during a press conference in the middle of the summit. “A cheap Europe could turn out to be a very expensive mistake. Security comes at a price,” warned Polish prime minister Donald Tusk. The budget fight always follows the same steps. The commission usually proposes a high budget, EU leaders demand huge cuts, the European Parliament then object to the cuts, and then falls in line after making some small gains. MEPs can certainly delay the adoption of the budget. But they won’t, even though they have warned that negotiations will begin, rather than end, once EU member states agree on their figures. So there is a lot at stake. Several leaders, including Dutch prime minister Rob Jetten, insisted there is no real deadline, but all of them know that pushing the talks deep into 2027 is risky. Read more Dutch dismiss any deadline on budget deal as EU leaders remain divided on size and new resources of revenue Officially, it is true: there is no end-of-the-year deadline. But Macron has warned that negotiations cannot drag on into 2027, when his country heads into an election in which far-right eurosceptic (and currently likely next president) Marine Le Pen has pledged to reopen any deal, reduce France’s contribution and stop Ukraine financing. A deal before deadline would protect the budget against later changes. Red lines?
